text: Love of The Holy one, blessed be He: There is no better trait than the Love of The Holy one, blessed by He, for the entire service of G-d and Judaism draws from it. To serve (G-d) from love is not comparable to serving from fear, as the author of the "Sefer HaBris" delved and expounded to explain the root of love and fear very well. "The words of the mouth of the wise is grace" (Ecclesiastes 10:12). Praiseworthy is the man who is diligent with his words. To make habit the work which is before me I will come in short, and I will write some notes for myself and for others in my condition, according to that which I learned from the book quoted earlier ("Sefer HaBris") and other books which I have seen to be a reminder between my eyes, and may G-d the Almighty assist me in the matter of honoring His name.

And behold, the love of The Holy One, blessed be He, is one of the 613 commandments. It is an ongoing commandment, which every person can fulfill at all times and at every moment through remembrance: it is fulfilled through thought and meditation alone, for when he brings into his heart that it is proper to love Hashem with a great love, he fulfills a great mitzvah. And behold, these commandments that are fulfilled by thought alone are easy to fulfill, for after all, a man is not able to exist without thinking for even one moment. And if he thinks foreign thoughts or evil contemplations instead of thoughts of love of G-d, blessed be He, and fear of Him, and the like, this is nothing but an evil heart — one which "abandons the fountain of the waters of life and hews broken cisterns" (Jeremiah 2:13). And in place of being able to do a mitzvah, which would give him reward, "the fools passed by and were punished". And therefore, it is proper for every man to strengthen himself with determination and fortitude to distance all foreign thoughts and evil contemplations, and implant holy thoughts even “running and returning”. And immediately upon realizing that they are not doing good by thinking foreign thoughts, they should feel regret, flee from them, and cleave to their Creator as much as they are able.

And behold, there are two types of love: one is love rooted in oneself, for when one puts into his heart how it is the way of man to love a person from whom he will see benefit, even little benefit, and all the more so if it was a great benefit, and even more so if [that person] gave him all his livelihood, fulfilled all his needs, and bestowed acts of goodness upon him, [in such a situation] he would say: “With what will I pay this man, who has acted towards me with kindness and given me gifts gratuitously? Even if I were to live a thousand years, I would not be able to pay my thanks to him; if he sent me great distances at midnight, I would have to heed his voice — I would not be able to turn him away empty-handed, due to how greatly I am indebted to him.” And if his friend saved him from a certain illness or great pain, or from a severe injury or loss of a limb, he would increase his love [for the friend]. And if he rescued him from death and revived him he would increase his love for him more and more. And in this manner, how many levels are there to love! [Each] higher and higher [than the last], and if one [mortal human who does you a single favor evokes great love], how many, many times more with a love compounded and multiplied is it suitable to love the Creator. For all of the goodness of the world — whether brought about by the hands of heaven or by the hands of man — all of come from Him, may He be blessed, for He is the one who places in the heart of his creatures [the desire] to do good to one another, and “the Omnipresent has many messengers”.

And if many evils and misfortunes passed over his head, and he was saved from them, he is required to love G-d the redeemer, the savior, and the one who responds and shows compassion at all times of affliction and distress. And all the more so, by kal vachomer, if the Holy One, blessed be He, dealt with him with kindness, that his eyes did not see evil and he was rescued from all the evils that were readied for him and that were brewing in the world — for he was rescued by [G-d’s] kindness, may He be blessed, and on this they said (Devarim Rabbah 2:37): “Every soul will praise G-d”, for upon each and every breath it is required to praise [G-d]. And now Israel will say, “With what shall I come before Hashem, shall I bow myself before G-d on high (Micah 6:6)? For he bestowed upon me innumerable and uncountable good. And even when we stand and provoke him to anger in his presence, he does not act towards us according to our sins nor does he deal with us according to our transgressions.” And let not the phrasing that we say in nishmat kol chai depart from his thoughts: “and even if our mouths were filled with song as the sea etc., …, in hunger you nourished us, and in plenty you sustained us; from the sword you rescued us etc.”. And he should count in painstaking detail how many, many goodnesses [G-d] bestowed upon him from the day he came out of his mother’s womb, and from how many evils he saved him whether they are revealed to him, or hidden from him in the manner that they said (Niddah 31a; Pesikta Zutarta Chukat 21:9): “There is no recipient of a miracle who recognizes his miracle, whether troubles came upon him and he was saved, or whether they were prepared for him and did not come — for all these a person is required to tale it to heard and love his creator with a fierce love”.

All of those benefits are trivial compared to the good for the soul, which is truly a great benefit, without measure. Therefore, let Israel rejoice in its Maker (Psalms 149:2), who chose us out of all the nations, and gave us a Torah of truth, and implanted within us eternal life, and sanctified us with His commandments, and chose us to serve Him and to bless in His name (Deuteronomy 10:8), that through these things, we will merit to live and inherit goodness and blessing for the life of the world to come, which is a great good, so much so that it was said: "A single hour of tranquility in the world to come is preferable to all of life in this world" (Pirkei Avot 4:17). And this is what one should think when one labors for the sake of reward. But when one reaches the level of being like slaves who serve the master not for the sake of reward (see Pirkei Avot 1:3), then one should rejoice more and more at the privilege of being a slave to a Sovereign lofty and exalted, majestic and awesome, whose grandeur is beyond understanding, and who selected us out of all of the nations and out of all of the heavenly hosts, who desires us and who loves us. And God wanted to credit Israel, therefore He proliferated Torah and commandments for them, and He is eager in His love, despite our being mortals like vain vapors (Psalms 144:4). This is a great and peerless good, to those who contemplate the grandeur of the Creator and contrast it with the lowliness of man. And through this, one will recognize and know, that it is a great benefit that He chose us and drew us to His service, so that they said in truth: "A single hour of Torah [sic] and good deeds in this world is preferable to all of the world to come" (Pirkei Avot 4:17). And one should consider what has been honor and greatness (Esther 6:3) for the lowliest of people?—That the king was eager for his honor (Esther 6:6-11), and chose him to stand before him and to serve him, even though he is flesh and blood, a fetid droplet, just like him—how much more so the degree of separation of the Omnipresent above us, up to a place that the power of our minds cannot divine, so great is the good that our Creator, our Deviser, our Maker, has granted us.

And in truth, what there is to be happy about regarding the good of this world and on being rescued from evils is that through life and the good [of this world], we have the ability to come to the great good, which is to serve our Creator. And this is the evil of misfortune and death — that they prevent us from serving our Creator, for in any case [the tragedy incurred] is the same. For our days are as a passing shadow, and the evils and the good of this world are fleeting; “Breath of breaths, everything is a breath.” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Yet we desire with life and goodness because it appears to us that it assists us in the service of the Holy One, blessed be His name. And this is the intention of what we say in “nishmat kol chai” after “and if our mouths were filled with song as the sea etc.”: “Until now, your mercies have helped us”. We wish to say, “You have gladdened us with all the goodness and saved us from evils in order to mercifully assist us in your service”.

And see that it is so: every single person, corresponding to how much the Holy One, blessed be He, helped them in their service of him, is required to love their creator for this great good. For the good that all of Israel as a whole has — that he gave us the true Torah; good laws and commandments — is not comparable to the good received by him who He gives strength, health, sufficient ability, calmness, tranquility, and security in the service of Hashem, blessed be His name. And as for him who has a place among those who sit in the house of study, he finds that he receives a great good above others. And for whom Hashem has bestowed wisdom and knowledge to act with good and upright character traits and who he caused to understand the disgrace of forbidden things and bad character traits so that he may distance himself from them, such that he will find favor and good understanding in the eyes of G-d and man (Proverbs 3:4) by being one who does what is right and good, this is a great good and precious beyond measure. Correspondingly, all are obligated to love their creator with a strong love proportional to the greatness of the good, and humble themselves greatly before him, and say: “I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all of the truth that you have done to your servant (Genesis 32:11). With what shall I approach Hashem and pay my thanks to him?” And these things the living should take to heart and expand and deepen in their minds pure thoughts until their hearts blaze with sparks of flame of love of the creator. And more will be written on this with the help of Hashem in the section “Joy”, see there since love and joy are one and the same.

And there is another type of love that comes from the side of intellect, and it is called “love of the sublime”.  For he who has a good mind, who knows the virtue of a perfect man and whose heart desires perfection, loves the perfect man for his perfection with a strong love. And all the more so should one love the Creator, blessed be He, who is the true perfection in all types of perfections in the ultimate perfection. But this love is not possible except for [those who are in some way] similar [to G-d], [i.e.] for those who desire good and walk in the path of goodness. And therefore, the more a person occupies himself with Torah and keeping His commandments, may He be blessed, that He, may He be blessed, established, because “the precepts of Hashem are upright” (Psalms 19:9), and walks in His paths, may He be blessed, will multiply his love for Him due to His perfection. And all whose hands grow weak from the Torah and from the commandments will turn back from the love of the Creator, as he has no similarity to the Creator, and further since his sins are themselves a dividing wall between him and his father in heaven. And [these sins] are the accusers and adversaries who confuse him with many thoughts until he will not remember, or will be unable to continuously maintain, his thoughts of love of the Creator.

And since we are “orphans [(children)] of orphans”, we are much impoverished and have increased in impurity and guilt, and have sinned, preventing [receiving] good from him. And we are unable to direct our minds to the fear and love of Hashem, the honorable and the revered. Therefore, it is good for one to set times to read daily, or at least from time to time, books that remind him of fear and love [of G-d] and the like, such as the holy book “The Beginning of Wisdom”, and the book of the pious Shelah [Rabbi Isaiah Horowitz, who wrote Shnei Luchot HaBerit, “The Two Tablets of the Covenant”], and “The Duties of the Hearts”, and. “The Covenant” and the like. And through [the words in these books], perhaps there is hope to fulfill, even a little bit, the commandment “to fear and to love [G-d]”, for fear comes from love. For proportional to [one’s] great love [for G-d], whether due to the good that he received from him or due to his sublimity and perfection, he fears going against his will and angering and grieving him. Also, the commandment of fear is fulfilled in one’s thoughts alone as is written further on in the entry “Fear”, and from the thought of love, the thought of fear will automatically be drawn.

And one is able to arouse their love and their fear in all physical matters and the like, such as eating or drinking something that is pleasing to the palate and in whose richness the soul delights, walking, hearing a pleasing voice, marital relations, gaining money (which surpasses them all) and the like. Let [each man] take to heart [the following]: “If I so love this thing, which is all fleeting, vain, and empty — which came in a night and was lost in a night (Jonah 4:10)— how much more so should I love the Creator, who is the fountain of all that I love and that gives pleasure to me — who gives me life and all my joys.” And he should turn his mind from loving the physical thing and cleave to the love of his acquirer [(G-d)], and the servant should clearly say  “I love my master (Exodus 21:5)! How beautiful and how delightful, love, with all its pleasures! (Song of Songs 7:7).” And so when he is afraid of some cause among the happenstances of time, he should take to heart and say “how vain is the fear of this thing, it would be much better if I feared G-d”. And he shall immediately replace and change this evil to good, and receive good reward and find redemption through this.

And as we’ve stated, the attainment of love and fear is entirely proportional to how great your actions and study of torah and mussar books [(i.e. books that discuss concepts pertaining to morality, such as this one)]. Likewise, you will grow in torah and mitzvot proportional to [your] love and fear. For love is etched from doing the will of one’s beloved with all one’s heart, soul, and might. Great waters are not able to extinguish love (Song of Songs 8:7). And proportional to the greatness of love, one bothers himself even with great trouble, and inclines his shoulder to bear upon [the] heaviness for many days, and it will seem in his eyes as if it were only a few days due to his love for the creator, just as [it is] for love of money and other loves. And if a person were to love the Torah and the commandments [just as much as] he loves money, his wife, children, and the like, it would be sufficient. If only the priest’s wife would be like the innkeeper’s! And by this he knows whether he has reached the level of one who loves his creator — if he rejoices over His word like if he found a great spoil (Psalms 119:162). And he will be careful not to waste even one moment by not engaging in Torah and mitzvot, even more so than he would distress himself over the loss of a massive fortune, for it is more precious than pearls, and all desirable things cannot compare to it (Proverbs 3:15). And in truth they say (Avot 6:2): “Woe to them, the creations, from the insult of the Torah!” For there is no greater insult than this: one who can reap a massive profit and bring joy to his creator, but does not care. And if he engages in laughter and idle talk, about him the verse says (Jeremiah 2:13): “The have abandoned me, the fountain of living waters, and made for themselves broken cisterns”. Happy is the man who hears and thinks about the reward of a mitzvah, that doing it brings joy to his creator, because one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is more beautiful than all of the life in the world to come. And one must increase his strength where there is financial loss so that he will not love money more than the Creator. And whoever neglects the love of their creator by not engaging in torah or performing a mitzvah that he has at hand for any reason, finds that his love of that thing is greater than his love of the Creator, and there is enough contempt and anger [in this]. And in all that he performs in this world he should think about the ultimate purpose — that doing so will give him strength in his service of G-d, blessed be His name. And all acts should be for the sake of heaven in line with what is written (Proverbs 3:6): “In all your ways acknowledge [G-d], and your paths will be smooth”. This is a core principle of the Torah, because through this he will not deviate from the path, and all his actions will be weighed with a balance, by measure, weight, and volume, and it was found that all his days he was only occupied with Torah.
And there are many types of love that are put on a person, and they are all drawn by love of the Creator. This [one] emerged first. And after:

Self-love - for it is a nature in man that the Creator instilled within him, that he should love himself. And [every] man is closer to himself and loves himself more than the entire world and than everything in the world, for everything a man has he will give for his life. But there is a grievous evil — that of the evil inclination — that holds ones eyes closed and makes him as if he were drunk and ill and can’t distinguish between left and right, and causes himself harm. From soul to flesh it consumes him in a way that no enemy in the world could possibly do more evil to him than he does to himself, and this is great folly. And in truth it says (Sotah 3:1): “There is no man who sins until a spirit of folly comes upon him”. Someone who is a fool, sometimes a foolishness will come upon them that causes them to destroy themselves intentionally [commit suicide], may we be rescued from this. And whoever has a brain in their skull will take to heart that it is proper for man to love his body and soul, [and through this] a good reward will be gathered for his toil — his soul will delight in abundance and his flesh, too, will dwell securely.

And according to common sense, it is proper for man to love his body more than his money, and better dry bread with peace and rest than riches with heavy burdens and troubles ([paraphrasing] Proverbs 17:1). And if Hashem expands his border, he should find an outlet for his money to find rest for his body, and not toil in this world for the sake of monetary gain unless it is good for his body. And he will be a kindly man [who through this] benefits his soul (Proverbs 11:17), provided that he is not among the heavy drinkers of wine, gluttons of meat, eaters of royal dainties, excessively wasting days and nights, [or] excessively engaging in marital relations like roosters, for all these will consume both soul and body (Isaiah 10:18), as will be further explained in it’s [proper] place. And above all it is necessary to protect oneself from anger, as is written (Ecclesiastes 11:10): “banish anger from your heart, and do away with evil from your flesh.”

And he who does not guard himself from everything that destroys his body, finds that he is an enemy to himself, seeks his own evil, and will be judged [for it]. For if one harms others, the sin is in his hands, and how much more so if he injures himself. And “he who troubles his own flesh is cruel”(Proverbs 11:17). And even more so one needs to guard himself from a place which has even the slightest risk of mortal danger. And if he enters a dangerous place for money, it turns out that his wealth is dearer to him than his life, and if a miracle is performed for him, it depletes his merits. And it turns out that he sells his merits and great goodness stored up for him in the world to come, exchanging the reward of mitzvot for money, which perishes and is destroyed. Further, he will surely be punished. And he is liable [to forfeit] his life as the words of the Merciful One warned: “Guard yourself and guard your body greatly (Deuteronomy 4:9), and guard your souls greatly (Deuteronomy 4:15)”. Therefore, no man should go to a dangerous place, such as on dangerous roads or through seas and rivers, unless it is absolutely necessary for his livelihood. And [in these cases] he should bring with him armed men in order to minimize the danger through natural means. And if he can go on dry land, he should not go by river or sea, which increase the danger. And proportional to the danger, one loses merit if a miracle is performed. And therefore all that one is able to do to minimize danger with money or extra effort, behold, such a person [who does this things] is zealous and will be rewarded, and the reward is greater than the expenditure. And the commandment to take utmost care of yourselves which he fulfills is sufficient to save him from all distresses and bring blessings upon his home. And he will remain intact in his body and intact in his wealth (and more is written on this in the section titled “Guarding”).

And the essence of love, that one loves himself, his body, and soul, must be drawn from the love of his Creator. Just like a person loves his tools and is careful not to dirty or destroy them because he loves himself and wants to use them, all the more so he must be particular about his body and soul to not dirty or destroy them, for they are instruments of service with which to serve the master Hashem. And should be his entire intent for guarding his body and soul; he shall execute his words in judgment (Psalms 112:5), and the Lord will be his helper, and will be his might.

The love of sons and daughters: The love of sons and daughters is necessitated by nature, for they are the bone from his bone and flesh from his flesh, and even "a raven cares for its children" (Ketubot 49b). But one must take care that his love does not overturn boundaries, that he does not make his son suffer and longs for him greatly and gives him extra love. Shlomo has already said in his wisdom (Proverbs 13:24) "One who spares his rod hates his son, but one who loves him rebukes him." And the essence of love is love of the soul, and included in this is love of oneself, for "the son gives merit to the father" (Sanhedrin 104a). As it is written (ibid 29:17): "Punish your son and he will give delicacies to your soul." Therefore, a person should be careful to behave with his son with open rebuke and hidden love, according to what he understands in his youth. "Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a youth, a rod of rebuke will distance him from it" (ibid 22:15). But the father should take care not to be cruel to his child and not to hit him and give him a bruise out of anger. Rather he should lead him with gentleness and with mercy he should hit his legs, not on a place where he will sustain a wound like between the eyes. And when he is older, "a rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding" (ibid 17:10). And it is known (Moed Katan 17a): that he who hits his adult son transgresses because of the sin of putting a stumbling block before a blind person, etc. This does not refer to an actual adult, rather according to the son's understanding and character traits" when he is older and does not accept rebuke, "a soft tongue breaks the bone" (Proverbs 25:15) and he will not be lenient in his own honor so that his reputation will not be ruined. And he [the father] needs to be even more careful with that which our rabbi cautioned (Shabbat 10b): One should not teach his son when he is among other boys, for "jealousy is as difficult as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6). The principle is: according to the mental ability and character traits of the son is how a father needs to behave with him in a way that he will not sin. If he does sin against him, he should be quick to forgive him so his son will not be punished on account of him, and he should not be exacting with them, and sometimes he should make himself like a deaf person who does not hear and as if he does not see, and sometimes he should submit his will to their will. And this is a major principle for one who wants to  bring merit to his soul and the souls of his sons after him.

And the main thing in order to give satisfaction to our father in heaven is to try with all our strength and might to teach our children Torah. And how good is the portion and how pleasing the lot if one’s children are torah scholars! That person will rejoice from the “offspring of his loins” [i.e. his children] in this world and in the world to come. And at the very least he must give his life and try with all his soul and might to ensure his children are not ignoramuses, for great is the evil of ignoramuses without understanding. For “there is a way which is straight in man’s view which ultimately leads to death” (Proverbs 14:12, Proverbs 16:25). And “a boor cannot be sin-fearing, nor can an ignoramus be pious” (Avot 2:5). And if he isn’t able to merit that all of his children have the crown of torah, at least he should have to himself one torah-scholar child for whom torah is his profession [i.e. that he studies torah full-time]. And he should pour out his soul before Hashem [to pray] that he has children who are masters of Torah, and flawless in their character and values. And at times he should fast for this, so that his sins do not prevent the good [i.e. Torah] from [coming to] his children. And most of all one needs to keep his eyes on his daughters, for man doesn’t know what the share of their portion will be. Therefore he must be careful to distance them from all bad traits, teach them all types of women’s crafts, accustom them to minimal sleep and to all good traits, and advise them well in how to act with their husbands in the upright and good way such that they find favor in the eyes of G-d and their husbands.

And every prudent man acts with knowledge, and his eyes foresee the thoughts and tricks of his children; and if he had the power, he would prevail to distance his son from “being a man that knows hunting” [(i.e. unlike Esau, see Genesis 25:27)]. And he should distance him from lies, for truth is the foundation of [all] building. And he should exert himself to distance his son from disgraceful things and from uttering oaths, and thus distance him from any trace of a prohibition, ugliness, and anything similar [Chullin 44b]. And in particular from the sins of youth one requires extra protection, knowledge, caution, and alacrity. And he should not trust his sons, nor should he be confident to say: “my son does not follow the advice of the wicked and does not stand on the path of sinners”, for there is no guardian against licentiousness (Ketubot 13b, Chullin 11b). And all who are greater than their fellows have a greater [evil] inclination than them (Sukkah 52a). And immaturity affects much, and evil companions affect much (Mishnah Sotah 7a). Therefore, one should greatly strengthen himself to distance his sons from [such] friends with all he has at hand, and to strive for them with all his might to ensure that they stay on the good road and observe the ways of the righteous (Proverbs 2:20). This is the core of the pain of raising children, and “according to the pain is the reward” (Avot 5:23). He will be happy from the product of his loins [i.e. his children] in this world, and his soul will rejoice in the world to come.

And also this love [for children] needs to stem from love of G-d, that he should endeavor to gather many workers for G-d, for this is the fruit of sons and daughters — that they do the will of their creator. Otherwise, they will be “children in whom is no faith” (Deuteronomy 32:20), and non-existence is better than the existence of evil [see Eruvin 13b]. Therefore, this must be his entire objective in loving his children: to fulfill the commandment of his Creator, to bring satisfaction to his Maker.

And one also needs to strengthen himself to arouse his love [for his wife] so that his children will not be the children of a hated wife, G-d forbid, and “according to the pain is the reward” (Avot 5:23). And the fence to prevent disputes from arising in the home is to not examine every household expenditure down to the penny, for a woman who is jealous of her peer is as difficult as Sheol [the grave]. Therefore, a man should increase the honor of his home as he is blessed, each thing in its [proper] time, and appease his wife, for blessing does not rest in a home except for the sake of his wife (Bava Metzia 59a). And peace at home is important to the point that it is permissible to dissolve the Great Name [of Hashem] to bring peace between man and wife (Nedarim 66b). Therefore one should greatly strengthen himself to remove evil from his home and to induce the Shekhinah to enter it.

And included in this love [of his wife] is that one should not wander [i.e. leave] far away on a distant journey for a long time, for besides the fact that he causes harm to himself, as will be explained in the section “thought” with the help of heaven, he also brings pain to the body of the wife. For “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6), and when her husband is separated from her, she is poor and afflicted; she lives a life of sorrow. At the very least he should be careful to appease [her] with words, with letters of peace to “soften the blood of love”. And according to what he can afford he should at times send gifts and pleasing things to his wife to revive her crushed heart, bring pleasure to her soul, and diminish her pain, and it will be considered as a great mitzvah whether [the gift is] small or large.

And even greater is the obligation of the wife to love her husband, honor him as a king among his troops, be in awe of him, and fulfill his desire and will with all her might. And all her focus and attention should be to strive to fully understand what her husband thinks and desires, and to do his will for the sake of finding favor in his eyes. And the essence of her love is love of the soul — she should devote herself to helping him in his service of Hashem, may He be blessed, for this is her portion. And with sweet lips she should speak to him if she needs to guide him on the good path, and to comfort him when he is in distress. And she should rise while it is still night to wake him up, and serve Him [Hashem] together, shoulder to shoulder in the service of Hashem, may He be blessed. And it goes without saying that she should be careful with all her might to not to be the cause of any harm that would prevent him from serving Hashem, may His name be blessed, G-d forbid, for that woman will bear her sin. What can I say, for not all temperaments are the same, except that everything is according to what kind of person he is: she needs to conduct herself according to his characteristics to find favor and good understanding so that their marriage will turn out well in love and brotherhood. The wisdom of women builds her house (Proverbs 14:1), and one who fears Hashem shall be praised (Proverbs 31:30). For besides needing to be modest, “the king’s daughter is all glorious within” (Psalms 45:14), so that she not cause men to sin through their eyes and hearts. And she needs to be adorned for her husband and be careful with cleanliness and purity and orderly with expenditures in order to not cause her husband to sin by turning his eyes to another. These actions too will bring her closer to him and make her find favor in his eyes

And behold, if a woman is given into the embrace of a G-d fearing man, and how much more so if he possesses Torah and greatness, she will naturally honor and love him with a great love. [But] indeed more encouragement is needed for the woman whose portion is a man with difficult character traits and temperaments, despised and insignificant among men, [and] lacking all good. [Even] for this she should not trifle his honor in her eyes and despise him in her heart, G-d forbid, rather at all times she should be careful to honor him, whether righteous or sinful, easy or burdensome, for the word of the King, the King of the world, is upon her. And what does she have to do concerning the hidden things of the Merciful One? For G-d sits and hand-picks marriages, and thus all that He put upon her to do, she must do. To what is this similar? To the man who who the king desires to honor, having appointed him as second to the king, and thus the entire nation is required to honor him even if he is a leper or a zav [i.e. has a bodily discharge], so too is the case here. And just as a woman should be cautious in the commandments of Niddah, Challah, and candle-lighting, so too should she be careful with honoring her husband, for thus the King commands her. And her reward will be greater, since her actions prove that she does these things for their own sake, fulfilling the decree of the King of the universe. And our rabbis of blessed memory say (Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, Chapter 9): “there is no virtuous woman among women except one who does the will of her husband”. And all women should take warning from the incident (Nedarim 66b) concerning Bava ben Buta and the woman who accorded honor to her husband and struck Bava ben Buta on the head in carrying out the will of her husband [in reality, the husband never intended for her to strike Bava ben Buta, and yet she was still rewarded for her efforts based upon her understanding]. And thus all women must give honor to their husbands, the great and small alike (Esther 1:20).

And there are women devoid of knowledge, that cause their husbands strife over household needs that he did not bring, and this is great stupidity. In any case, if the husband is poor and doesn’t have the means for something, his [own] grief, pressure, shame, and humiliation are enough for him, for he is ashamed to reveal to his wife that he doesn’t have the means. And the wife must be sensible to ensure that she does not add to her husband’s pain, but rather, on the contrary she should comfort him with the sweetness of her lips and tell him: “do not be sorry about your empty purse, for Hashem will not spurn forever [Lamentations 3:31], and there will come days in which there will be delight, in which we shall be sated with bread and be well-off. Or there will be pleasure that our tables are full of abundance in the World to Come, for not all merit to eat from two tables [see Berakhot 5b], and this world is fleeting and empty. Rise, my father, eat your bread with joy, for also on bread alone does man live [play on Deuteronomy 8:3]”. And she should speak good words like these to him in favor and kindness, until he his happy and gives thanks for his portion, for the good fortune that fell to his lot.

And if Hashem broadens her husband’s means, and yet he remains stingy with household needs or delays in bringing them, what concern is it of hers? She puts what he brings in front of him and he eats it. Will he be able to say to her “why haven’t you made the delicacies I enjoy”? She will say to him “how can I make that which you have not brought?” And if she makes a quarrel over clothing, jewelry, and worldly pleasures, this too is vain and vexation of spirit, for “better is dry bread and quietness with it” (Proverbs 17:1). And if the great name [of Hashem] written in holiness can be erased for peace in the home (Nedarim 66b), how much more so does the husband and wife need to dissolve and nullify their wills for the sake of peace in the home. And the wife should sense that her husband isn’t as well-off as she thinks and doesn’t wish to tell her that he doesn’t have the means, since he thinks this is bad luck for her, and similar sufficient reasons he may have for not fulfilling her will. Therefore she should not press at the time nor force him against his judgment to increase his spending against his will and not to his benefit. And likewise she needs to sense when her husband is angry at her over nothing, for perhaps he suffered in the market and was greatly angered over something that happened, as the people say: “able or unable, he quarrels with his wife”. And she must tolerate it, and not enrage him or distress him further.

And this is a great principle: if there is contention between people or between husband and wife, and one was the one who “opened the waters” initiating the argument [i.e. opened the floodgates for further contention] (Proverbs 17:14), and went out of line and opened his mouth without restraint, even if he can overpower his opponent, he should not say a word at the time of his anger, whether good or bad. Rather, wait until the time passes, and after a day or two admonish him in-person peacefully and fairly and with calm language, and say to him: why have you done this? What is my crime or sin that you have pursued me with more and more anger though I have no violence in my hands? Is this good in the eyes of G-d? And similar good words. One who does this loves peace and pursues peace [see Pirkei Avot 1:12] , and “there was peace in his army and tranquility in his palaces” [see Psalms 122:7]. They are the pillars of the world. As our Rabbis of blessed memory say (Chullin 89a) on the verse (Job 26:7) “he hangs the world on nothing [blima]”, that the world stands on he who restrains [bolem] his mouth during an argument, for by this the argument will be barren, not giving birth [to further conflict].

And a woman whose lot has fallen to an evil and worthless man, who strikes and curses [her], who forces himself upon her [I.e. demands intercourse. This does not mean that he physically forces himself upon her, but rather pushes and demands], should take upon herself the judgment of heaven. She should suffer and not lose heart as atonement for her soul, for she will be well-rewarded in the world to come. And a woman of valor, an intelligent wife, will not reveal her husband’s disgrace and his bad temperament and nature to others, and her voice will not be heard, in order to not debase her husband and to not add to his hate of her for revealing his disgrace, for then his nostrils will smoke, and his anger will flare, and he will strike her even more severely. And especially she should not reveal anything of her mistreatment, distress, and pain to her father, mother, or brother. For what will [good] she find in the pain of her father, mother, and brother, that they will suffer heartfelt anguish, until a fire burns within them over the pain of their daughter? [Then] they will go out with weapons, and fight with the husband until the flames of their strife are fully kindled, and the woman will bear her sin. And she will eat the fruits [i.e. bear the consequences] in this world: she will be hated by her husband and he will add to her mistreatment for revealing things between him and her.

And thus her father, mother, or relatives, if they have sense and understanding, even if the suffering of their daughter was revealed to them, however great, they should act as if they know nothing, and receive her husband with a pleasant countenance for the sake of their daughter. And even if they want to raise their voices and argue with him, they should find a way to make it appear as if the report came from the neighbors, who heard it through the window, and the like. And even better is if she [the daughter] doesn’t reveal anything as we said, in order to not pain them and cause them to hate him [the husband] in their hearts. Instead, she should act as a wife who has found peace in her in-laws’ house and eager to go tell its praises in her father’s house, and she should say to them that all is good in her home. And it will be accounted to her as a mitzvah that she brought joy to the hearts of her father, mother, and relatives, and she [will thus] be worthy to be protected and granted a good outcome. And even greater is if she rebukes him herself at an opportune time with pleasant speech, grace, and kindness. Certainly this [sweet speech] produces more fruit, for it is truly said (Proverbs 25:15): “a soft tongue breaks the bone”. And she should also pour out her soul before Hashem every day; perhaps Hashem will show her favor and her prayers will bear fruit to return her husband to the good path, and thus she will also find rest.

And included in the love of a wife for a husband, is that she prays for him before Hashem, for a woman’s prayer comes from the tenderness of her heart, and her tears come readily. If she shouts to Hashem in the walls of her heart, certainly her prayers will bear fruit. And thus a woman must pray for her children, for [when] her husband and children have peace, she will have peace, and who will have more compassion for them than her? (And if G-d will be with me, I will arrange a book of women’s affairs as I desire, [there] I will also write prayers pertaining to women with the help of heaven). In light of this, she should be careful and guard herself invoke [heavenly] judgment upon her husband and to not shed tears because of him, even though a greater obligation [to not cause her pain] is placed upon him, as our sages of blessed memory say (Bava Metzia 59a [see also Rashi]): A man must always be careful about mistreating his wife, because, since she is prone to tears, the punishment for mistreating her is quick to come. But she too should take this to heart, for if evil befalls her husband, G-d forbid, she will be among the first to suffer, and she will have harmed her own soul. Let everyone hear and fear [because of] what happened in the Talmud (Ketubod 62b) to the wife of a certain rabbi [Rav Rehumi], that she was waiting for her husband to return from his journey, and after he didn’t come, she shed two tears due to her pain, and immediately her husband died  on her account [the roof he was sitting on collapsed due to her tears] even though he did not mistreat her nor mean to cause her pain. And it seems that there is a moment of [divine] anger that causes a man to die due to a light manner, may the Merciful one save us from this. Men should therefore tremble to not cause pain to their wives, and women should fear crying on account of their husbands. Rather, they should seek mercy for them. These are some of the proper paths of a husband and wife that are pure, and the wise one will hear and learn. And there is more in the book “Shevet Mussar” by Rav Eliyahu HaKohen, may his memory be for a blessing, in the first chapter concerning conduct between husband and wife, see there. And so they will do and add this to their conduct in the good path according to their personalities, so that the Divine Presence may rest between them and peace may be in their home.

And this commandment is the task of the father and mother of the wife to advise [her] before marriage and afterwards, to do these and similar things, and to be very careful with the honor of her husband, father-in-law, mother-in-law, and the brothers and sisters of her husband, and his brother’s wife and sister’s husbands, and all of his relatives, for the honor of Hashem, that commanded her to be careful with honoring her husband. And this is all because honoring her husband’s relatives is work that gives satisfaction to her husband, and [thus] she finds favor in his eyes, and it will be counted as a mitzvah for her. And as we mentioned already, it isn’t necessary to hasten to love peace and pursue peace except for those from whom peace has escaped, and they have legitimate reasons to quarrel, on these falls this commandment to pursue peace to honor the Lord of Peace [see par. 9]. But the wife must be careful to not be careless, not to increase conversation and laughter and general lack of seriousness, and all the more so other forms of emotional closeness with her husband’s relatives. Rather, she should be honorable and modest in her in-laws’ home both at home and outside, and not to cause anyone to sin, for due to this sin women are cursed to die young, give birth to corrupt children, or have their sons and daughters die whilst still little. But the cautious merit to have descendants, proper and holy, who reach old age, joyful and glad.

Love of Torah scholars and those who fear heaven and contemplate His name — Love of Torah scholars, those who fear heaven, and contemplate His name also stems from love of G-d, for one who has a faithful friend, he also loves his [the friend’s] children and household. And furthermore since he deeply loves his friend and seeks his welfare with all his soul and all his heart, everyone who benefits and brings satisfaction to his friend he also loves. And further, we have already said that reason obligates anyone who is similar to him to love an admirable person, perfect in character and understanding—whether he himself possesses admirable qualities, or merely loves perfection even though it is not present in him. Thus, for all these reasons, it is considered proper [lit. they sought] to arouse love for Torah scholars, those who fear Hashem, and those who contemplate his name (Malachi 13:15), so they should be as dear [to him] as the pupil of his eye. And behold the reward of this, as our Rabbis of blessed memory say (Shabbat 23b): “He who loves the rabbis, will have children who are rabbis”. And the essence of love is in the heart, but one needs to also express it with action. If Hashem increases his means, he should support Torah scholars with all his soul and might [wealth], and he should both act and cause others to act. And if he doesn’t have the means, in any case he should personally fullfill [the principle that it is] “greater to serve [a Torah scholar than to study under one]” with all his strength such that [the scholar] will be able to observe the Torah and do his service without difficulty. And great is one who causes others to act, more on which will be written below. And it goes without saying that one must guard his soul greatly to not pain a Torah scholar and [to ensure that] no Torah scholar finds a reason to resent him, as the teaching already elucidated (Pirkei Avot 2:10, Midrash Tanchuma Yitro 12): “come and warm yourself by the fire of the sages, but beware of being singed etc.”

And if it is a great obligation to love Torah scholars even though they are not relatives, since they are all like relatives, even more so, if the Torah scholar is a family member, one is obligated to love them with an even greater love. And it is the task of the brothers and the relatives [of the scholar] to support him even more so and with greater strength so that he may remain devoted to the Torah and do his service [of Hashem]. And this will bring them praise, renown, and splendor. And in this way they honor the [deceased] father since he will receive spiritual satisfaction through his son the Torah scholar. And they too will have a portion, [for] this is the portion of each person in all of their labors, and it is found that they did kindness for [both] the dead and the living. “Happy is the man that does this, and the son of man that holds this” (Isaiah 56:2). “She is a tree of to those who lay hold on her, and happy are those who hold fast to her” (Proverbs 3:18)

Surely, one should not view a Torah scholar as small in his eyes because he provides for his needs, G-d forbid, nor should he give himself credit for sustaining and supporting him, for [the torah scholar’s] portion rests among [the benefactor’s] assets, as is said on the verse (Exodus 22:24): “to the poor among your people”: it is [merely] the mission of the Merciful one that he is doing. And not only this, but what the poor person does for the rich benefactor is greater than what the benefactor does for the poor person, for it is a merit for him [the rich person] in the world where all is good, as our Sages of blessed memory say (Ruth Rabbah 5:9, Vayikra Rabbah 34:8) on the verse (Ruth 2:19): “the man with whom I did [kindness] today was Boaz” [that is, Ruth said she did kindness to Boaz despite him giving her food], therefore one should be very careful about [the recipient’s] honor. And also the Torah scholars must be careful with the honor of their rich brethren who benefit and support them. For if it is said (Eruvin 86a) that Rabbi [Yehuda] and Rabbi Akiva honored the wealthy even though were not dependent on them, how much more so is one who needs them and benefits from them obligated to not be ungrateful, to show them some respect, and to exert himself somewhat on their behalf to give them satisfaction. Extra affection should be shown to them, and [the scholar] should teach them “the proper way to go and the deeds they should perform” (Exodus 18:20). With pleasant conversation and sweet language,  “open rebuke is better than love” (Proverbs 27:5). And he should share in their distress and grieve with them and pray for them, and he should always pray for them so that they will succeed in all they undertake. And in all their Torah study and good deeds, they [the scholars] should have them  [their supporters] in mind as well. Regarding this and similar matters, “the wise man shall hear and increase learning”(Proverbs 1:5), and he shall do so that he may find favor and good understanding in the eyes of G-d and man.

Love of fellows - It is well-known how great a virtue love of neighbors is, to the point that our Rabbis of blessed memory said (Jerusalem Talmud Nedarim 9:4) “Love your neighbor as yourself” -  this is a core principle of the Torah, and our Rabbis of blessed memory explained (Shabbat 31a): their intention is to say “what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor”. And behold, in proportion to the greatness of the good [of this virtue], so too does a person’s evil inclination grow stronger against him all day, until, because of our sins, [particularly] through the sin of baseless hatred, our cities are destroyed, our Temple lies desolate, and we are exiled from our land. Yet the Satan still dances among us, accusing us. Every person turns to his own gain and does not worry about the misfortune of his fellow, and there are those who delight in their distress, and those who for the sake of enjoyment, however slight, swallow one another alive. Woe to the eyes that see such things! For our eyes will fail from waiting - we have waited for salvation, but there is no savior as long as this trait is found among us. And thus one must strengthen himself to arouse this love [for others]. And the particulars of love for one’s neighbors has already been explained extensively in “Sefer HaBerit”, and I will present it briefly. And it is, that one must rise to the principle of “turn from evil and do good” (Psalms 34:66): one must turn from evil in speech and actions.

Regarding speech - what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend. One must be careful to guard oneself from saying to his friend, or about his friend, anything that he would not want said about him — this includes harmful speech [lashon hara], verbal mistreatment, and many similar things. And likewise in this manner one must turn away from evil.

In practice, [one should] not harm another or cause him any damage — [that is,] anything that he would not want others to do to him. And one must delve deeply into this, because the deceptions of the evil inclination are many. And even more so one must be careful in a situation where there is financial loss, for one is prone to be lenient for himself and be drawn to the profit even at the expense of his friend.  And thus it is not in vain that [the sages] say (Eruvin 14b) [source incorrect in the text, really Eruvin 65b]: “a man is recognized by his purse”. Happy is the man that fears Hashem and loves Hashem with all his might [wealth] and does not incline after profit.

And similarly one must fulfill the mitzvah of “and do good” in speech and in action. In speech, [one should] say good and proper things to make people happy: for example, by sharing good news, giving good advice, and removing obstacles from another person’s path, [i.e.] by informing him if one becomes aware that any harm may befall him in any way, and comforting him in his time of distress, and many other similar things. And in action, one should perform acts of kindness, both physically and financially. Just as one would want others to act for him, and to have mercy upon him, and inconvenience themselves to have mercy on him, likewise he should act in order to perform acts of kindness and fulfill the mitzvah of loving your neighbor as yourself. “Happy is the man who does this and the son of man who lays hold on it” (Isaiah 56:2). “According to the pain is the reward” (Avot), for according to the pain one gives satisfaction to his creator. And just as a father has compassion on his children and “a brother is born for adversity” (Proverbs 17:17) [see Rashi there for what this means], so too each person should help his fellow, for “we are all one man’s sons” (Genesis 42:11); we are brothers. And just as one cares for one of his limbs, so to one must care for every person of Israel, for all of us are like one person; like one body.

And see, a person loves himself, his son, and his brother because his nature requires him to. But when it comes to his friend, in a case where he thinks that there is a financial loss or physical exertion [in helping him], his love for himself overpowers him. And all the more so because the matter is a great mitzvah, a person’s [evil] inclination grows stronger against him to cause him to pass over the will of his Creator so that he should lose a great good. [Thus] one must strengthen himself against his [evil] inclination, be concerned for the honor of his Creator, and awaken the love [within himself]. And fortunate is Israel! How much effort they exert, and how many burdens they endure, and how much money they spend for the sake of mitzvot and good deeds, how meritorious is their portion! But here lies the problem: there are great mizvot that no one seeks out since people do not consider them as being such important mitzvot. And if it is said (Avot 4:2): “Be as quick in performing a minor mitzvah as a major one”, for you do not know the reward given for the mitzvot, even more so with a mitzvah as great as [loving a fellow],   which has included in it love of kindness and love of fellows and the ways of peace, it is proper to pursue it like one who pursues life [itself]. And since the [evil] inclination is [always] close, producing forty-nine arguments to declare the creeping creature pure and to favor one’s own self-interest, and all the more so because this matter involves several considerations, such that one who fears the word of Hashem is confused and does not know which way is the path of light, the recommended counsel is to carry out the teaching of the Tanna that said (Avot 4:14): “do not rely upon your own understanding”. And this is a core principle of the whole Torah, and all the more so in monetary matters, “He who walks with the wise shall be wise” (Proverbs 13:20), and he will reach the paths of life.

And the core of the mitzvah of love is in the heart, that one must not rejoice in the misfortune of his friend, G-d forbid, rather one must be happy in his successes and distressed over his pain until the point that he prays for him. And the way to acquire this love is to take to heart the following teaching of the Sages (Chagigah 15b): that even at the time the wicked are suffering the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) is distressed, what expression does does he utter? etc. And from this [we learn] that when a person is comfortable, the Shekhinah is also comfortable. Therefore, a person who loves G-d ought to rejoice in the joy of the Holy One, blessed is He, and the Shekhinah, and to be distressed in its suffering. And further, when a person is at ease and has wealth and things, he will not be prevented from increasing in mitzvot and good deeds, and [in this] there is satisfaction for our Creator. This is not the case with a person in distress, whose “heart is not with him”, and he falls short in the service of Hashem, may He be blessed. And poverty undermines every good quality, and therefore [he may] transgress the will of his Creator and cause bitterness to the one who brought him into being.

And from all that we have said, a wise person will understand that one should rejoice greatly when he sees people doing the will of their Creator, and should feel deep distress in his soul over those who commit transgression. And even if he himself falls short in his service of the Creator, he should not desire that his friend also be like him, so that “the trouble of many will be the consolation of the fools”. To what can this matter be compared? To a noblewoman who has ten sons, and the king commanded them to provide her with food and support her and provide her with everything that she lacks.  And it happened one day that one of the king’s sons violated the decree and did not give his mother the portion [that was due of him]. Even though he will surely be punished, in any case the son loves his mother and is pained over failing to provide his portion, [and] he will surely at ask whether at least his brothers fulfilled their obligation, for in this will be half of his comfort. And if they say that all of them acted treacherously as he did, his sorrow for his mother will increase as she cries and sobs because she was left in hunger and thirst, utterly destitute. And the lesson of the parable is self-evident. And further one should rejoice in the good of his friend since the many blessings will increase the [observance of] mitzvot and good deeds, and through the increase of the performance of mitzvot and good deeds, good comes to him as well. For his sins will not tip the entire world towards guilt, for he will surely be punished for all the harm that he causes. And when goodness increases through his fellow, the world tips towards the side of merit; on a good day he too will enjoy the good.

And behold, King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 10:12): “hatred stirs up strifes, but love covers all sins”. And there are causes due to which hatred arises between a man and his brother [fellow], and all is vain and chasing after wind. There is one who hates [another] because the other person sinned against him physically, financially, or [by diminishing] his honor; therefore regarding this the Torah has already commanded (Leviticus 19:18): “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge”. And [the sages] explained the reason for it: for that person is constrained in his actions, and is carrying out the will of the Merciful One. For Hashem told him to curse, and his unfortunate lot caused it so that the guilt [of this action] came about through a blameworthy person. And therefore, there is no room to hate a fellow, for he is like an acts in the hand of one chops with it, and “why does a living man complain, a man over his sins?” (Lamentations 3:39). And there is one who hates [another] because of his jealousy, and thinks that because of his fellow, his livelihood has been diminished. And this is nothing other than a lack of faith, as will be discussed in the section “Faith” with the help of Heaven. And there is one who hates [another] since he sees that his fellow is not walking in the good path, and in this the living person should take to heart that he too has shortcomings and blemishes according to his own level. For everything is according to what kind of person he is; “the scales and balances of judgement are in the hand of Hashem” (Proverbs 16:11). And if his fellow’s [evil] inclination overpowered him and he transgressed the will of his Creator, and Hashem extended kindness to him and guided him on the path of truth, surely he ought to give thanks to Hashem and to be careful in the fine details of his commandments to a hair’s breadth according to his knowledge and understanding and according to the help that he received [from Hashem]. And he should not despise or hate his fellow in his heart, for it was not permitted to hate [anyone] except a wicked person, who even after being rebuked several times nevertheless persists in his rebellion and provokes our Father in Heaven and causes sorrow in Heaven. But regarding any other person, it is forbidden to hate him. And the Tanna already spoke very strongly in condemning hatred, to the extent that he said (Avot 2:11): “Hatred of people removes a person from the world”.

And the great fence for removing hatred is through fulfilling the statement of the Tanna who said (Avos 1:6): “And judge every person on the side of righteousness”. And even if your eyes see the evil in the wrongdoer, you should not blame him to the extent that you hate him, since a person’s way is upright in his own eyes, and what was he supposed to do? A person does what is right in his own eyes. We can’t do anything other than pour out our soul before Hashem, that he should correct him by offering him good counsel, and that he will lead guide him in paths of righteousness for the sake of his name. And if one will say, does the Holy One, blessed be He not punish the man that walks in the stubbornness of his heart and what is right in his eyes because he should lear and did not learn, you [should] say to him: that applies to one who is exacting [with others], [then] they [Heaven] are exacting with him as well. But one who does not insist on his own due [i.e. overlooks offenses even when halachically he is allowed not to], all of his transgressions are overlooked (Yoma 23a, Megillah 28a), and with the measure that one uses, so too do they measure him (Megillah 12b, Sotah 8b). Rather one should not hate his fellow if he doesn’t walk in the good path, for if so one should hate himself even more, for who would dare presume in his heart to say that he investigated extensively, and that everything within his power to do he did as was fitting for him to do? Consequently, he is no better than his fellow. And perhaps the other person is better than he is relative to his level, understanding, and ability, as is known from the statement of the sage that honored every man and said “if he is wiser than me, it is fitting for me to honor him due to his wisdom, and if he is duller than me, it is proper to honor him for he is better than me, since his sins are unintentional and mine are willful”. And similarly, along these lines, a person should take to heart various pure thoughts to drive away hatred and awaken love [for others]. Behold, his reward is with him, with the measure of goodness increased.

And behold the truth that our Rabbis of blessed memory said (Bava Metzia 33a): [Between] his lost object and his father’s or teacher’s, his own takes precedence [if he had to choose between which to recover]. But as they already said (Bava Metzia 33a), all who are fastidious in this will in the end come to that. And Rashi explains, if one is always exacting in this, [that is], looking out for his own benefit, he will thereby cast off from himself the yoke of acts of kindness and charity and in the end will need other people. Rather he needs to be willing to lose a small amount so that his friend should not suffer a loss, or that his friend should gain a great deal, or to save his fellow from trouble, and through this Hashem will command blessing upon him.

And the main essence of love of friends is that one should “clothe himself in the body of his fellow” [i.e. put himself in his friends’ place], in such a way that even if he is not particular about his [own] honor and humiliation, nevertheless he should consider [the matter] as though he were like his fellow, according to his character traits. [He should consider how] he would want [others] to honor him, and not say to him anything [involving ] verbal mistreatment, and not infringe upon his honor. So he should do to his fellow. This is the general rule of love of friends, and in this “Hashem gives strength to his people, Hashem blesses his people with peace” (Psalms 29:11).

Mourning - Mourning over the destruction of the Beit Hamikdash [the Temple] is something that depends on action, and especially during the period of the Three Weeks, by day and night [one should] place ashes on the place where the Tefillin are laid, sit beside the Mezuzah, and recite the order of the Tikkun Chatzot. In truth, the action is not the core [of mourning], rather one must have an eye that weeps bitterly and a broken and crushed heart — like one mourning for his mother, gloomy, he should sigh with “brokenness of the loins” [i.e. being crushed by grief] over the sorrow of Heaven. And all is proportional to one’s knowledge, greatness of love [of Heaven], and the reward of his soul. And see the truth is that we are greatly diminished, and there is no one among us who knows what we are lacking, what we have lost, what we have caused through our many sins, what the exile of the Shekhinah is like, and [the extent of] the suffering of the upper and lower beings. Over this, all who are sorrowful should grieve, [but] in any case every man isn’t obligated except according to his [own] capacity. And he should imagine as though his mother were girded with sackcloth, wearing black [garments] and wrapping herself in black [garments], crying out bitterly — a voice heard in Ramah [on high, but see Jeremiah 31:15 snd other verses] — moaning like a dove. What does the language say? (Sanhedrin 46a): “I am distressed about my head, I am distressed about my arm”. “I have reared and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me” (Isaiah 1:2). And like this and that the living should take to heart things that embitter the heart. He should pour out his soul with a wailing voice; perhaps he will merit to see the consolation of Zion and the rebuilding of our Temple and our glory, that it be speedily rebuilt in our days, Amen.

And from the conclusion of the matter [in this paragraph], you will hear how bad and bitter the actions that a few men and women do are, who gather together to rejoice in social merriment on the nights after Shabbat and other nights, particularly in the winter nights, and indulge in frivolous merriment, eating, drinking, playing music, and singing songs of lust and of idolaters. Woe to them! Woe upon them, since without a doubt their joy will be turned into sorrow, either in this world or the world to come, if they do not take to heart to return [that is, do teshuvah]. For besides the several prohibitions that they transgress — [such as the prohibition against sitting in] a gathering of scoffers and obscene speech in sensual songs — our Rabbis of blessed memory say (Sotah 48a) “an ear that listens to song will be uprooted”, and further, “A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bore him” (Proverbs 17:25), for the Holy One, blessed be He will say, “Oy! Cruel children! A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping; Rachel is weeping for her Children” (Jeremiah 31:14). And she is like a maiden girded with sackcloth, “and Hashem will roar from on high, and from His holy habitation He will raise his voice; He will roar mightily over His dwelling place” [Jeremiah 25:30]. And the angels of peace weep bitterly, and all the host of Heaven on high, the righteous and the pious, and our righteous Messiah are weeping and mourning, and all over the destruction of the Temple that was destroyed due to our sins, and we at that time will be sitting and singing, rejoicing and making merry in social revelry — this is nothing except evil-heartedness and blindness. Whoever is fearful [of Heaven] and tender-hearted, upon hearing words such as these, should take to heart not to go anymore to social revelry of this sort, or even to a non-obligatory meal. Rather, “in all labour there is profit” [Proverbs 14:23], and he should not rejoice except in the joy of a mitzvah, and through this Israel will rejoice in its Maker.

And included in the commandment of [someone] mourning is that when a dead [relative] of his dies whom he is obligated to mourn for, is that he should be careful to fulfill the laws of morning as proper, as our Sages of blessed memory established, [and] as is explained in Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah Chapter 342. And many ignorant people do not know to be careful due to a lack of knowledge, and study words of Torah, wear leather shoes, and seek to distract themselves from the mourning. And the wise should be prudent, for at the time when the forces of judgement are upon him he must be careful to fulfill every matter properly and to accept upon himself the judgement of heaven. And he shall surely weep for the three days [designated] for weeping; a living man should complain, a man over his sins [Lamentations 3:39]. And for the entirety of the seven days, one should occupy himself with eulogizing [the deceased], recounting the virtues of the deceased and every good quality that was found in him. And he should study the laws of mourning, or sorrowful [Torah] words, in such a way that he does not shift his thoughts from mourning, for [the sages] prohibited even engaging in childish chatter so that he won’t divert his attention. And when he fulfills the words of the Sages, he is assured that he will not continue to grieve anymore. And it is fitting for every person, when a misfortune befalls him, G-d forbid, to seek books on the laws of mourning. And if he doesn’t know the holy tongue (Hebrew), he should seek books in foreign languages, like the Shulchan Aruch in another language and the book “Me-am Lo-ez” on Parshah Vayechi [Genesis 47:28-50:26] and the like. And this is the whole [purpose] of man, that he should seek to know what he should do according to the law, from the mouths of Sages or from books, and he will not transgress the will of his Creator, and through this there will be joy in his dwelling.

And specifically over one’s father and mother it is proper to show increased mourning in all twelve months, and not to go to [any] revelry or feast, and not visit any [other] person, whether for Shabbat or festivals. Consequently, he should increase his study for their rest and the elevation of their souls, and he should not go out to stroll at all, and should always think: “perhaps they are suffering, and here I am enjoying myself”. And one should not say, “What [good] will my mourning over them bring? Can I bring them back through this? Of course not!” For they said in the Aggadah, which was brought by the Ramban of blessed memory in the book Torat HaAdam (page 27b), that Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, said “Joshua, put on black [garments], and cover yourself in black, and be careful regarding the honor of this downtrodden one”, see there. This teaches us that everything that demonstrates mourning over the soul’s passing is an honor to it. However, one should not follow the custom of certain places that wear weekday garments on Shabbat, even on the Shabbat that falls within the seven [days of mourning], according to the words of the Rav, the Arizal of blessed memory, from whose mouth we live. The righteous should hold firmly to walk in the holy path, for all His ways are justice, and His words are life.

Faith - Faith, “it became the cornerstone” [Psalms 118:22]. For the one who has faith in Hashem, whose glory fills the whole Earth, and whose eyes are open upon all the ways of human beings, to repay each person according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds. A righteous person shall live through his faithfulness, because certainly he will be careful in the fulfillment of all the commandments and their precise details. And he should be eager in [performing] the commandments, and careful to be clean from every sin, and exert himself like a lion for the service of his Creator, and not back down in the face of anything. For his eyes will see, and his heart will understand, that the name of Hashem is called upon him, and His eyes range about the whole Earth. An eye sees, an ear hears, and all his deeds are recorded in a book [Avot 2:1]. And he should feel ashamed before him, and serve Him with a perfect service — with fear, love, and great joy. And he will believe with complete faith that there is a good reward for the righteous, according to the greatness of the deed, and according to the difficulty is the reward [Avot 5:23]. And the punishment for the wicked is severe and bitter, over all of their transgressions, and a balance and scales of justice are in the hand of Hashem, to repay each person according to his ways — according to his level, understanding, and ability, and according to the effort and the joy, as two battle lines are set opposite one another.

And there is yet another fence for faith, from which come many good qualities — namely, to believe in [Hashem’s] providence, may He be blessed, over the lower beings in every single detail, and that “no person bruises his finger below unless they decree it upon him above” (Chullin 7b). And both good and evil come from the mouth of the Most High, whether by the hand of heaven or by the hand of man, for the Omnipresent has many messengers, for good or for bad. And “he gives you power to be successful” (Deutoronomy 8:18), for “not to the wise [belongs] bread, nor to the swift [belongs] the race”. Consequently, one should not be concerned for the loss of his money when it comes to serving his Creator and doing his will, and he should not exert himself to become wealthy through something forbidden. Rather, he should conduct his affairs with judgement, properly and uprightly, according to the Torah. And he should not become angry, flatter [others], hate his fellow, take revenge, or bear a grudge, for he knows and believes that Hashem said to him, “Curse”, and everything is from him, to diminish his liability [for sin], for his own benefit. “A G-d of truth and without iniquity, he is just and right” (Deutoronomy 32:4). “Hashem is righteous in all his ways, and gracious in all his works” (Psalms 145:17). And all that the Merciful One does, he does for the good (Berakhot 60b). And thereby one should take upon himself the judgement of heaven with joy, and not loathe rebuke.

And the root of everything is to trust in all the words of the Torah and of the Sages. And if his understanding cannot accept [something they say], he should attribute [the difficulty] to a deficiency of his own knowledge, and the limitation of his comprehension, trusting completely that all of their words are living, enduring, and trustworthy forever and for all eternity. Come and see how profound the words of the Sages are, for they said that the entire Torah is contained and embedded within the quality of faith. And many say with their mouths that they are believers, descendents of believers, but their actions contradict [what they say], and the action comes and overrides the speech. And for everything, G-d will bring him into judgement for having walked in darkness. Aside from the punishment for the transgression himself, there is also another [punishment] — he will surely be punished for being among those who are lacking in faith. Or if he does believe, and nevertheless does not take care to walk in the proper path, this is brazenness and the forehead [i.e. shamelessness] of a harlot.

And behold, these commandments — to believe in Hashem’s existence and in his providence — are counted amongst the 613 commandments. And these mitzvot are ever-present, in that one can fulfill them at all times and at every moment through thought alone. Behold therefore it is good for a man to keep this on his lips and not forget it in his heart, and from time to time the Israelite servant should say, “What is [the matter] with you, my [evil] inclination? Will you always pursue me? Hashem will rebuke you, Satan, for I am a Yehudi son of a Yehudi [on the significance of Yehudi, see Megillah 13a], and I trust with complete faith in the existence of Hashem, who is before me always, and in his providence over each individual down to the finest details, and that he pays a good reward for the slightest good thought, statement, or action, and [metes out] a harsh and bitter punishment for every evil action, even for light speech and for every evil thought. See therefore that it is proper for me to do such and such, to behave in this way in this manner, and to withdraw my hand, be careful, and keep myself away from such and such, until my conduct becomes pure and upright, in thought, speech, and action, [so] that there should not be found in them anything devious or crooked, so that my faith should not prove false. Thus I will do and I will not deviate [from it].” And such and such things the living should take to heart, and should keep them constantly in his mind, and delve deeply into them, at length and breadth, to walk in the paths of faith. Then his hands shall [themselves] be faith — [that is], hands that demonstrate that his faith is genuine [through doing actions that show his faith]. Thus faith is good, to merit the life of the World to Come, a secure resting place, and, above all, to bring pleasure before the One who dwells in His abode.

Eating and Drinking - Eating and drinking fall into three categories: commanded, permitted, and forbidden. And it is possible for one to make all of his meals a commanded meal when these conditions are met — conditions stated in truth by the Sages from whose mouths we live. The first is that he must intend in his eating that he should be healthy and strong for the service of G-d, blessed be His name, and to fulfill “the merciful man does good to his own soul” (Proverbs 11:17). That is to say, to separate out and bring to light all the sparks of holiness that are attached to everything he eats and that he drinks. And one must pray for his food before every meal, and this is a great obligation as explained in the Zohar (Exodus, page 62). (And I the insignificant one have arranged a text of prayer, to express the intentions we mentioned, because there is benefit in uttering them verbally, to help the heart remember. It will also help bring holiness upon the eating, especially [when] one’s intention is for the sake of Heaven, and I placed it in Beit Tefillat). And see what is written in the holy book “Reishit Chochmah” (Gate of Holiness Chapter 15), with one’s own eyes they will see the intentions of eating, which correspond in their measures with the sacrificial offerings. Happy is one born of a woman who has the means to build his upper chambers in the heavens through his meals, provided that he direct his heart toward Heaven, and do these things according to halakhah. And “one of clean hands will increase in strength” (Job 17:9) — [that is,] he should be careful with washing the hands properly according to the enactment of the Sages.

And he should clothe himself in awe when he comes to bless his Creator who prepared his food and other pleasures [he enjoys] — how very careful one must be to recite the blessings as enacted, letter by letter, word by word. And all the more so when mentioning the Name of G-d — all his bones should be seized by trembling. For it is the King, the Lord of Hosts, high and exalted that he is blessing, and if he is not careful, G-d forbid, he blasphemes Hashem, and the [quality of the] words follow the intentions of the heart. Thus one must be careful in all blessings, particularly in blessings pertaining to things one enjoys, and even more so in the blessings over bread which are a Torah obligation. Just because it is long, it should not be hurried, rather it should [be recited] in order as prescribed and in accordance with Halakhah.
