And this is something that common sense dictates and the eye sees in the ordinary way of the world, even in the blessing of a commoner, all the more so when he comes to bless the King of Glory, awesome and fearsome, who in his great kindness allowed us to bless him and remember his name, honored and awe-inspiring. And the commandment will be accounted for us, and he will establish for us reward and blessing for our blessing, thus we must be careful to say [the blessing] as per Halakhah. And a fence for this is to say every blessing with a loud voice, for the voice spurs intentionality, and he will know with certainty if he blessed, and not be in doubt, and he will merit and cause others to merit to answer “Amen” after him, and those who are not proficient will learn from him. And one must also be careful to uphold the words of our Sages of blessed memory to dip the piece of bread in salt three times, and he should not transgress this when possible, for all their words stand at the heights of the world.

And one must sit honorably at the table, for he eats at the table of the King. And [we see this in] the well-known story about Rav Rabbi Yisroel Najara, [which took place in] the time of the Ari of blessed memory — he would sing at the table with a sweet voice, and ministering angels would gather like at the festivities of a bride and groom. And his arms were exposed due to the heat, and a voice from Heaven descended [saying] “flee from this man, who diminishes the honor of Heaven, for he doesn’t sit honorably at the table that is before Hashem”, and immediately they all departed. And the Ari was looking at this great sight from his home, and he revealed his secret to Rabbi Yisrael Najara, and he trembled greatly, and he made himself presentable and sat honorably, and he sang as before, and the ministering angels returned and gathered as before. Therefore, one who fears the lord should [have his] entire [body] “speak honor” [i.e. be presentable]. And one must be careful to eat with manners, and not like the ravenous and the gluttonous about whom it is said in the holy Zohar (Pinchas, Folio 246): they are from the side of Esau, as it is written concerning him (Genesis 25:30) ‘please feed me’, and he is despised and rejected in the eyes of G-d and man.

And likewise, one must be careful to eat [only] until he is satisfied, and he should not fill his belly to [the point of] bloating the stomach with coarse [i.e. gluttonous] eating, for there wickedness settles — everyone who goes on [his] belly builds a dwelling place for the evil inclination. For so wrote the Kabbalists, that whatever one adds [to his eating] on a weekday beyond the amount needed for his satiation adds strength to the “Other Side” and strengthens his evil inclination so that it may overpower him. And all the more so, one who indulges in optional meals and social merriment adds great strength to the “Other Side”. For just as a mitzvah is elevated and adds strength to the heavenly retinue when it is performed by many, by the same token, a transgression that is committed by many is magnified and adds strength to the “Other Side”. And the sages of Mussar have already written how many harms one who eats more than [the amount] needed for his satisfaction causes: 1. He transgresses the prohibitions of “do not destroy/waste”. Furthermore, he wastes the time [he spent] eating, and the time of relieving himself. And if the stomach becomes upset and he will be preoccupied [because of it], then [there are] three periods of time [lost]. And if he becomes ill and dies, then he is responsible for his own life. Thus one who guards his body should distance himself from eating and drinking excessively — he should not eat except when hungry, and he should not eat until he is completely full, but [he should stop] a little before. And as the Ra’avad wrote, one who withdraws his hand from food which is pleasant to his palate for the atonement of sins, it is considered as though he had fasted, and as [though he had offered] a sacrifice of atonement (Rabbeinu Yonah in the book Yesod Hateshuva). And this person is prudent, for he eats to satisfy himself, yet [because he restrained himself from excess] it is considered as though he had fasted. And one who eats for the sake of Heaven should not pursue that which is pleasant to the palate but harmful to the body — rather, [he should choose] that which is beneficial to the body even though it is not so pleasant to his palate. And even more so one should refrain from excessive drinking, for it is a fire [which] consumes until destruction, and mighty are all that it has slain. Many drank, they drank “shod”, [and] devastation [shod] and destruction [came] within their borders. It is bad for them and bad for the world. And already the Sages spoke at great length in condemning them. And specifically the Torah scholar, the pain is greater if he drinks, and departs from proper conduct among the common people, for the Name of Heaven is desecrated through him. And fortunate is the discerning person who conducts his affairs with judgement.

It is written (Proverbs 32:2): “and put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite”. How very much one must be careful [to avoid] any trace of prohibition connected with eating! For it is found that the body is nourished through something forbidden, and the soul becomes guilty — he goes from evil to evil, for “her impurity is in her skirts” [Lamentations 1:9], and she will not be able to attain the paths of life, to fear and to love Hashem, the honored and awesome, and to serve Him with a perfect service. Therefore one must be careful and diligent, and keep watch over the slaughterers, that they be trustworthy, proficient, and greatly G-d fearing. And he should urge the members of his household that they should very thoroughly inspect as much as they are able regarding the prohibition of worms [in food], and not eat a fruit in which worms grow until he first cuts it open and inspects it. And likewise one must be very careful about the mixing of mosquitoes and fleas and all kinds of tiny creeping creatures that fall into food during the summer days, even without one’s knowledge. And one must be proficient in the laws of wines and foods regarding contact with non-Jews, and [the laws of something] having been out of sight, and the like. And how good and how pleasant it is to conduct oneself with restraint, and to flee from a hundred gates of what is permitted, in order not to enter through one gate of what is forbidden. For “all the labour of man is for his mouth” (Ecclesiastes 6:7), and “he who guards his mouth and his speech keeps his soul from troubles” (Proverbs 21:23).

And one must be careful not to be strict to  [i.e. become upset at] his household members over anything, and included in this are matters related to eating, even if she burned his cooked dish and did not make it in a way that suits him; he should not treat an inadvertent act as [if it were] intentional, and something unavoidable as if it were done willingly. And he should not be angry at his wife, servants, or the members of his household, for the way which one measures is the way Heaven judges him, and it is written (Job 11:13-14): “If I would reject the claim of my male and female servant when they contend with me, then what would I do when G-d rises and calls [me] to account. What would I answer him?” Reflect deeply on this and overlook [offenses] in your own standards, for more than your wife and servants are obligated in your honor and your service, you are liable in the honor and service of your Creator.

And one must be careful to say words of Torah at the table, and not let [the meal] pass without saying [passages of] Scripture or Mishnah. And when he is in the company of people, if he is capable of doing so, his mouth should utter wisdom to bring merit to himself and to [the] others with him, and if he is not capable of doing so or if circumstances don’t work out for him, in any case, he should learn privately, by himself, some Mishnah that is fluent in his mouth, like “All Israel [has a share in the World to Come]…” or “Rabbi Chaninya [son of Akashya says that the Holy One wished to make Israel meritorious etc.]” and the like, and whoever does more is praiseworthy. And since the Holy Zohar greatly emphasized (Exodus 157b) the praise that reaches above [in Heaven through] remembering the Temple at one’s table and being distressed and worried over its absence, I have therefore made it my practice to say this Baraita at the table in order thereby also to fulfill the obligation of [saying] words of Torah — It is taught [in a Baraita]: Rabbi Yose says, “one time I was walking on the road and entered a ruin, one of the ruins of Jerusalem to pray etc.” (Berachot 3a). It is taught [in a Baraita], Rabbi Eliezer says, “there are three watches of the night etc.” (Berachot 3a). “Yehuda son of Teima says etc.” (Avot 5:20). And on Shabbat I am accustomed to say the Mishnah of Yehuda son of Teima and the teaching “Rabbi Yohanan said in the name of Rabbi Yose, whoever delights in Shabbat, they give him an inheritance without boundaries etc.” (Shabbat 118a). “Rabbi Chananya son of Akasha etc.”.  And the words should follow the intentions of the heart, at a time of sadness [one should express] sadness, and at a time of joy, joy.

And for he whom Hashem has expanded his borders [i.e. given him material wealth], how pleasant is his lot if he is careful to give a portion from his meal to the poor who lacks someone to provide for him, [then G-d] will grant him abundance in this world and in the World to Come. And how good is it to raise a male or female orphan in one’s house, for in this one’s righteousness endures forever in each and every meal. And for him who lacks the means, he should intend to fulfill this by feeding his sons and daughters, for this too is called engaging in charity at all times. And on Shabbat and festivals it is proper for every man to preside over his table — he should raise his voice to honor his creator with the grace [of his voice] that [G-d] has endowed him with.

One is liable in mayim aharonim [rinsing the fingertips with water after a meal of bread] in the house and outside, in sitting and in going. And many have transgressed and have done away with the washing, and especially travelers. And one must be even more careful with washing the hands before eating, and he who transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death (Berachot 4b), and proportional to the pain/effort is the reward.

And in a mitzvah meal one must be careful that their gain [is not overshadowed by] their loss through some matter that is not proper, such as scoffing, contentious speech, verbal mistreatment, jesting, frivolity, and the like. Rather, the fear of heaven should always be upon him as a covering, and through this his eating will be accepted as a burnt offering. And when he behaves properly according to the Torah, his table will be an altar of atonement.

And one must say the Birkat Hamazon [blessings after a meal on bread] with pleasure and with a loud voice and with gladness of the heart. For when he takes to heart the words that come out of his mouth and concentrates on them deeply, it is impossible not to rejoice. And as is revealed in the words of the Holy Zohar (Exodus Folio 218), there is a great need and obligation for one to do everything possible to recite Birkat Hamazon with joy. And a great fence for intention, is to say the blessings with closed eyes or facing downwards and the heart [directed] upward. And one should have intention in the four blessings corresponding to the four letters of the [Divine] Name to cause an abundance and blessing to flow in the four worlds — Atzilut, Beriyah, Yetzirah, [and] Asiyah. Happy is one raised by a woman who merits this! And as is written in Sefer Hahinuch (Mitzvah 430), there is a received tradition that whoever is careful regarding Birkat HaMazon, his sustenance is readily provided with dignity all the days of his life. Go and infer from the reward that [through the blessing after meals] he gives great satisfaction to his Creator, and let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.

Truth - “The lip of truth shall be established forever” (Proverbs 12:19). And [truth] rescues from death, as is known from the Gemara (Sanhedrin 97a:6), in that place, whose name was “Truth”, [where] there were no lies and no man died before his time. And our Rabbis of blessed memory say (Sanhedrin 92a:19), that one who alters his words is regarded as one who worships idols, as it is written (Genesis 27:12) “and I shall seem to him a deceiver”. And Hashem is a G-d of truth, his seal is truth (Shabbat 55a:12), and his Torah is truth, and “the remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity, nor speak lies; neither shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth” (Zephaniah 3:13). And there are many ignorant peoples, that have taught their tongue to speak falsehood, and it has become to them as though completely permissible, to the point that there are those who lie in meaningless stories, without any benefit [to themselves]. Concerning them the Scripture says, “woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood” (Isaiah 5:18). And when [the falsehood] is in order to obtain some benefit, such as [cheating] in measure or weight and the like, then it is not called “falsehood”, but rather “diligence”, “cleverness”, and “effort”. And they say that whoever does not lie nowadays will not be able to earn [a livelihood], but they have answered falsely [i.e. their claim is false]. For our Sages of blessed memory said, in the Midrash on Proverbs (Midrash Tehillim 7:11; see also Yalkut Shimoni, Exodus section 56 and Psalms section 638), when Noah entered the ark, falsehood also came to enter. [Noah] said to him, “go out and find yourself a mate”, for all who came into the ark came male and female. He went and searched, and found destruction. He said to her, “do you wish to marry me?” She said to him, “what will you give me?” He replied to her, “whatever I earn, I will give to you.” And from then onward, whatever Falsehood earns, Destruction takes for herself. And if the evil inclination has made [the matter] appear smooth and attractive in his eyes, and shows him that he profits greatly through falsehood, in the end, without doubt, loss will come upon him, as is written in the Prophets: “One who acquires wealth, but not justly — in the midst of his days he will leave it, and at his end he will be a fool” (Jeremiah 17:11). Or [it will be] wealth preserved for its owner to his detriment, in this world and in the World to Come, “and G-d will withhold no good from those who walk with integrity.” [Psalms 84:12].

And the evils of lying are evil both in the eyes of G-d and man, since a liar is wretched and despised. And the disgrace of this matter is apparent to everyone to the extent that even among the nations of the world there are those who are very careful to speak truthfully and to not speak falsehood. And those who speak falsely in business dealings they conduct with non-Jews cause a desecration of Hashem’s name, for the non-Jews say that it is known that a Jew is a liar, deceiver, cheat, and similar evil things, and they [cast a] blemish [upon] sacred things. And the severity of the prohibition of desecrating Hashem[’s name] is known, and how many [more] prohibitions are entailed by falsehood according to the circumstances, as the discerning person will see. And such is the punishment of a liar, that even if he tells the truth others don’t listen to him.

And truth is the foundation of the edifice. And it is is known what they related in the Midrash (Otzer Hamidrashim page 2299), that a certain person was completely wicked, and through his taking upon himself not to speak falsely, he repented. For if he was going to commit a transgression, he would think: if they ask me, what will I answer? If I tell the truth I will be ashamed and humiliated, and if I lie, I would transgress what I took upon myself. And through this he restrained himself and did not walk in the council of the wicked, and did not stand in the path of sinners. And due to the great virtue of truth, and the great disgrace of falsehood and the evils that result from it, it is proper for a person to exert himself to educate his children in the virtue of truth, and from him they will see to be stringent about speaking the truth and will do as such. And he should watch over them so that deceptive speech should not be found on their lips, and if they do something that is not proper, he should see to it that they admit the truth. And then he should forgive them on that occasion and not strike them, rather he should only admonish them not to do it again. And if they lie, he should strike them severely for their lie. And he should make the sin of falsehood grave in their eyes, so that the children will tremble and be exceedingly careful, until it is their nature to not speak falsehood.

And included in the trait of truth is to make his words true — [to ensure] his “yes” is true and his “no” is true. For besides the prohibition involved [in lying as above], it is a shameful thing to go back on one’s word. And it is said (Bava Metzia 44a), “He who exacted punishment from the generation of the Flood and from the generation of the Dispersion will in the future exact punishment from one who does not stand by his word”. Thus one should think greatly before words leave his mouth if he can uphold them, and if he uttered something, [he should observe] “that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep” (Deuteronomy 23:24), as if he swore an oath.

And since our Holy Torah is a Torah of truth, how very much must one be careful to utter it in truth, to acknowledge the truth, and to accept the truth from whoever says it, even the smallest of the small. And they have already said — the rabbis, admitting [the truth], this is their praise. And one should not turn to a path of lies, to “burdens of falsehood and deceit” [Lamentations 2:14], rather truth should instruct one’s path. This is the upright path in which all the upright walk, and in this is found favor and good understanding in the eyes of G-d and man. And more is written on this below in the section “confession” and the section “falsehood” and the like, for such is our way — to return [to a subject].

Resoluteness - Resoluteness is a great necessity in the service of G-d, blessed be His name, for how many times does one violate the will of his creator due to a soft heart and pity. And a good man conducts his affairs justly (Psalms 112:5) according to the Torah and does not turn from the things that the Torah and the Rabbis of blessed memory command him [to do] to the left or to the right (Deutoronomy 17:11). Thus one who sees his friend doing something improper and out of concern for [his fellow’s] honor and the like remains silent, or at times is concerned about losing his own benefit and flatters him, such things are truly cause for anguish. And it is known what our Rabbis of blessed memory said (Proverbs 12:10), “the mercies of the wicked are cruelty”. And they said (Eruvin 21b, Eruvin 22a) on the verse (Song of Songs 5:11) “black as a raven” — you do not find words of Torah except in one who blackens his face over them like a raven and in one that makes himself cruel to his children and to the members of his household like a raven. And it is written (Proverbs 23:13-14) “do not withhold correction from the child… thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from She’ol”. And as the masters of mussar have already written, that women who show tenderness towards their children and prevent their fathers from hitting them, of them the verse says (Lamentations 4:10): “hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children”, for they caused that in the end [the child] will inherit Gehinnom. And on this, the wise [with] eyes in his head and a mighty heart should watch strictly and uphold the words of Torah and the words of the Sages properly, as required. And one who does this is amongst the students of Abraham our father, for although he was a merciful father, the perfection of the attribute of kindness, he made himself cruel to his only son that he bore in his old age, and took a knife to slaughter his son (Genesis 22:10) to do the will of his creator. And compared to slaughtering a child or giving up a life, everything else will weigh triflingly, and he will not refrain for any reason. This one should take to heart to stop himself from doing all evil and uphold every good thing, and this the whole of man.

The Land of Israel - The Land of Israel is the beauty of Israel (Ketubot 113a). It is known how great her virtue is, as is illustrated in the Holy Zohar (Section 3 Page 72) and other holy books — that whomever Hashem will choose He will bring near to Him to behold the pleasantness of Hashem and to contemplate in His temple. And every man must have his eyes and heart [directed] there every day, along the lines of which is written (Psalms 42:3) “my soul thirsts for G-d, the living G-d; O when will I come to appear before G-d!”. And thus one must try with all his strength to affix his residence in the Land of Israel, only he should first open his eyes [and carefully consider the matter] so that he not come to regret his earlier [decision], and so that he not have to turn back and leave. And a safeguard for this is that one should not go except in old age, after his wife has ceased to have “the way of women” and no longer bears Children, and he should not bring the young children with him, whether sons or daughters. And if G-d has enlarged his borders [i.e. given him the means], he may bring a daughter, because she is married off and he is thereby relieved of [supporting] her, but a son he should not bring at all, because the young family multiplies, and he does not know what a day may bring forth. And it is true that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise, but according to what our own eyes see, a person’s livelihood is difficult in the Land of Israel, and for the most part they are compelled to leave, to the point that they eagerly seize the opportunity for a mission undertaken for a mitzvah, to go out to foreign cities for about ten years or more. And they will live lives of hardship — they themselves, and their wives even more, and great are the dangers suffered by travelers both to the body and soul, as is well known. It is not so with those who live outside the land of Israel — they find enough for their livelihood in their own place, and when an elderly man and woman go [to the Land of Israel] as is proper, they will be able to live there to a good old age, and even if they live a life of hardship, it will be considered a good life in view of the abundance of [spiritual] good.

And it is a great mitzvah for children to try with all their might [money] and all their soul [body] to bring joy to their fathers and mothers by sending them to the Land of Israel, for this is a greater honor than thousands of gold and silver [coins]. And thus one must assist with great strength and determination if one of their brothers wishes to establish their residence in the Land of Israel. How great and how pleasurable is the dwelling of the brothers who help him, for he is their brother in flesh, and it is written (Isaiah 58:7) “do not hide thyself from thine own flesh”, and great is one who causes others to act.

And since many unpleasantries can result from serving as an agent and authorized representative for those traveling to the Land of Israel — for one must litigate with others in one case after another over a dispute that is not his own, and at times he may have to cause the foot of a person who is already somewhat tottering to slip — what need has a person for such trouble? It is true that this is a great mitzvah, but “the wise man’s eyes are in his head”: he should foresee the end of a matter from its beginning, so that he will not later regret what he first undertook, and every prudent man acts with knowledge. If he can excuse himself where there are others available, how good that is. But if not, he should know what he is to do and the path in which he should walk, and he should make his arrangements in such a way that he is likely to gain merit and unlikely to suffer loss. Everything stated above, however, concerns an unrelated person. But a brother is bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh. Therefore, an obligation rests upon his brothers to come to his aid, and they cannot simply declare themselves free of responsibility.

And it is the duty of one whom Hashem has expanded his borders, to not hold back from supporting those going to Israel since the hand of Hashem has bestowed good upon him, both [by supporting them] at the time they move and sending them gifts [of food/money], and a great mitzvah will be accounted to him. And it is true that it appears at first that it is not proper to go from city to city and burden the congregation since they must help their journey to the Land of Israel. And people murmur about them, saying: “Who asked this of them, that they should burden others in order to go to the Land of Israel? If they do not have [the means] of their own, let them not go.” After all, how many wealthy men, and how many rabbis — great Torah scholars of the world — rest honorably outside the land [of Israel]. Is this mitzvah greater than the mitzvah of lulav and the like, among the 613 mitzvot of the Torah? And nevertheless, one who cannot afford it is not obligated, nor does he go begging from door to door in order to fulfill it, for in truth they said (Berakhot 6a): “If a person intended to perform a mitzvah and he did not perform it due to circumstances out of his control, above it is written as if he did it”. And they said (Shabbat 118a) “Make your Sabbath like a weekday rather than become dependent upon others”.

And if he is an afflicted individual, that G-d torments, who has many troubles and pains, it is true that traveling to the Land of Israel is a necessity for him to alleviate his suffering and salve his wounds. But apart from this it appears that the actions [of those who beg to go to the Land of Israel] are improper and there is no room to pity them. But since we see that not everyone does so, rather there is [only] one in every city whose spirit is stirred and, whose soul desires it, and who acts upon it, this is a sign that this [desire to go to the Land of Israel] is from Hashem — that Heaven has granted him this merit. “The feet of a man are responsible for him; to the place where he is demanded they lead him” (Sukkah 53a). And it is proper to assist with all one’s strength to do the will of our Father in Heaven.

And as the Halachic authorities have already written (Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De’ah 251), that what they said regarding the principle of “the poor of your city take precedence” [i.e. should be given charity first], also apples to the poor of the Land of Israel, for they are [also] called the poor of your city in truth. They sit there like roosters in their coops — they are unable to earn a livelihood and there is no one found to take pity on them. Their eyes are turned those who live outside the land [of Israel], from letters to know how well their relatives are, to gifts to sustain their souls and gladden their hears. And great charity and kindness is done by the one who writes to them and who sends them gifts, whether a little or a lot, “every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing that the Lord has given him” (Deutoronomy 16:17), and a great mitzvah will be accounted [to him]. And it is good for one who writes to a different city to write and mention everyone from the other city who live with him in his city, for at times through the letter others [in the other city] will know of the wellness of their relatives and it will gladden the hearts of the afflicted, and he shall receive a blessing from Hashem and from people, and his mitzvah will endure forever.

And primary purpose of going to the Land of Israel is repairing the nefesh, and the ruach returns to G-d who gave it as it was given, and the neshamah praises G-d, as the sanctity of the place and the rest from the troubles of the time are a great help for this matter [of rectifying the nefesh/ruach/neshama]. Therefore, one who merits to go there should be holy and saintly [i.e. abstaining from indulging in worldly pleasures]. And even if Hashem enlarges one’s borders [monetarily], he should not overly indulge in worldly pleasures — rather he should live a life of hardship, conduct himself in the ways of repentance, and [walk] in the ways of piety. And he who is not an expert, should walk at the side of a wise person and learn from him — he will guide him in the paths of righteousness, and righteousness will be the belt around his waist. And he will shrivel and it will be good for him — let him take from the body and add to the soul. And he should be careful with all his might to uphold the commandments applicable to the Land [of Israel] with all his soul and all his might, for this is all the fruit of living in the Land of Israel. And the pure man, the rabbi who wrote the book “Haredim”, has already gathered at the end all of the mitzvot that apply to the Land of Israel.

And it is known that sins in the Land of Israel are punished double the sins outside the land, for it is the palace of Hashem. As such every “master of the soul” [i.e. pious individual] should pity his soul — night like day he should be attached to [Hashem] and to His Torah, without rest. And he shall atone for himself for that which he sinned against the soul (Numbers 6:11) all the days of his life, for it is time to show her favor, and to keep oneself far from idleness. Instead he should be holy, letting the hair grow [similar to a Nazir], for the obligation of [the] man is great. In sum it should be literally like Yom Kippur to them every day that they live on the land. The fear of heaven should hover over them, and great is the power of prayer in that place — the desirable land. And they already have awesome prayers which they pray on behalf of all the people of the Diaspora, and by their mouths we live. And each person should pray for his relatives according to the eloquence of his tongue. And he should pray for the rebuilding of the Temple, for the ingathering of the exiles, and so that G-d, blessed be His name, redeem us with a complete redemption speedily in our days, Amen. And I the poor one have already arranged a prayer, and added it to [my book] Beit Tefilati. And one who lives in the Land of Israel must be constantly joyful in his constant mitzvah, and all the sufferings should be light in his eyes through his love for [the Land].

One must be very careful with the blessing of God, not to recite a blessing in vain or an unnecessary blessing. For [if he does so], he transgresses, "You shall not take [the Lord, your God's name in vain" (Exodus 20:7). And you find this with an ignoramus who wants to be pious and recites a blessing over every single thing; and they sometimes stumble and fall with the prohibition of a blessing in vain or an unnecessary blessing. 'So the one who walks with the Sages will become wise.' And likewise concerning blessing (greeting) one's friend, it is written (Proverbs 27:14), "He who greets his fellow loudly early in the morning shall have it reckoned to him as a curse." And there are two ways this [happens]. The first is that there is a prohibition to say hello to one's fellow or to greet him before prayer [in the morning] since it is considered as if he is making him into an altar. And the second way is if he greets his friend in front of others and causes evil to [his friend], as the others will jump on him, since they will think that it would be fitting and good that he benefits them much more than he benefits this one. But [his fellow] does not imagine it so, and his heart does not think so for various reasons known to him. So it comes out that he caused for there to be arguments and grudges against him. Hence, 'every clever man should act knowledgeably.' So in any place where there is a concern that some damage will be caused to his fellow in any aspect or way - if he knows the thing, 'a trustworthy soul keeps a confidence.'

And it is hence an obligation incumbent upon a man to have mercy on his soul and on the soul of his daughter, to make efforts with all of his power to seek quietude for her which will be good for her and for him in this world and in the world to come. So, from time to time, he should pour out his soul in front of God for his sons and daughters, that God should arrange a proper match for them. (And I have already written a prayer for this, and have attached it to my house of prayer.) And also if the daughter herself knows to write or to read from what is written — her father should go to a rabbi, that he arrange a prayer [for her]. (And, with God's help, I will lift my hand for this [task] as well.) Or she herself should privately cry out from her soul in front of God, with words that come from her heart according to everything that comes out of her mouth, and pray to God that he should arrange a proper match for her. [She should pray that he be] a Torah scholar and that she be given into the lap of one who fears God, and that her match work out well. And prayer is a big [thing] in this matter. Go out and learn from Leah, who was Esau's portion. Yet by way of crying greatly, to the point that Leah's eyes became soft, she landed in Jacob's lot (Bava Batra 123a) and merited to bring out six tribes from which the splendor of Israel came out, houses of priesthood, of the Leviteship, and houses of monarchy.

YOUNG MAN- It is written- (Ecclesiastes 12:1) "Remember your creator in the days of your youth" For then is the ideal to serve your creator, for it is when a man has [ideal] might and strength to [give for] the Torah, to labor with all his strength on the deliberation [of the Torah] and to make ones nights like days, [maintaining only] minimal sleep. Then (i.e. his youth) he will be free, with no burdens. His consciousness will be clear and settled, able to understand, discern, listen, learn, and teach.  Since he has no preoccupations, especially if he is relying on his "father's table"- [meaning] a  complete lack of preoccupations, whatever he learns will be "indented" in his brain. As the saying of the sages (Ethics of the Fathers 4: 20) "One who learns in his childhood to what is he comparable? To ink written on fresh parchment, clear and sustaining". This is the Torah that remains (lit. stands) with Torah Scholars in their old age when their consciousness is settled. For Torah [learned] in youth is the "yeast in the dough", the foundation stone.

Behold it is so (i.e. the proper approach) for a desirable Young Man who is involved in Torah, to value this precious length of time (i.e. Youth), and not sway (lit. lose) from it even for a mere moment. He should "gird his loins" to engage in the Torah with all his might. For on this time [of youth], it is said (Tractate Megillah 6b) "[one who says] I worked hard but didn't find [success]- don't believe him". While all periods of man's life are precious, and every moment lost is a great loss with no reconciliation, still this period is most exemplary of all of them. As per the statement of the Rabbis, ( Tractate Shabbos 152a) "Youth is a crown of roses". [In conclusion] It is proper to be scrupulous on its value and that of his master's honor.

And there is stealing that is not considered stealing by the laws of people, but is considered stealing by the laws of heaven, such as one who decides in one's mind to enter in judgment with one's friend in order to collect money from the friend without doing violence, just because one's eyes deceived him, and one brings monetary damage to the friend, even without a fight or misuse, just by the simple emotion, having clean hands, and even if from the decision the friend would be forced to pay all, the spirit of the Place does not abide with him, and does this as a tax owed by the friend, one transgresses "love your neighbor as yourself" which is a general rule in the Torah, and it is in instances like this that they said "a person is known by their pocket" (Eruvin 65b). And according to the basic material, stealing is forbidden and the teshuvah is difficult, behold it says "one who steals even a cent from one's friend is likened to one who stole the soul from the friend, and the soul from the friend's sons and daughters" (Bava Kamma 119a) and while the stolen money is in one's hands there is no possible atonement, and it is very difficult to return food that was stolen (Chulin 99a). And behold a person who fears Hashem will be cautious and will guard oneself very much from anything that is forbidden in any aspect it can exist, and will deal all one's business faithfully, and even when a good opportunity appears, and those who sell are being stricken with harsh punishments, one will never extend one's hands towards stealing God forbid, because it is better for a person to die of starvation than to become an evildoer even for an hour in the Place's eyes, and "those who seek Hashem do not lack what is good" (Ps. 34:11) because God does not withhold good to those who walk in simple ways.

Might: Might is a large topic in the Torah. "Who is mighty? The one who conquers his [evil] impulse" (Avot 4:1). And happy is the one who overcomes his impulse like a man, to run after every commandment and flee from sin (Avot 4:2) and from all bad traits and to practice every good thing and matters of piety in all of their details, enhancements, and particulars in thought, speech, and action, with all of his heart, all of his soul, and all of his ability [alluding to Deuteronomy 6:5], and to be resilient-spirited, which is better than being a mighty man [alluding to Proverbs 16:32]. He also needs to practice the ways of repentance, afflicting his body, and many other things like this. Anyone who is attacked by his impulse and conquers it is called a mighty man. And even though the evil impulse is fire and it makes war with [its] tricks, and there is no day and no hour that it does not renew itself and overpower a person, any man or woman whose heart dedicates them to fight with it with the assistance of the Omnipotent can certainly [overcome] it. And it is only the beginnings that are difficult, and then it becomes easy for him and pleasant for him, and he will feel enchanted.

Exile: Our rabbis, may their memory be blessed, said (Avot 4:14), "Exile yourself to a place of Torah." Although it is true that our rabbis, may their memory be blessed, [also] said it is a proper thing for a person to live in the place of his ancestors and that a man who migrates from his place is like a bird migrating from its nest, so it is impossible for a person to uproot his home from his dwelling place, nevertheless, if it occurs that there is a need to uproot his home from his place — in the way of their statement, may their memory be blessed (Bava Metzia 75b), "One for whom it is bad in this place, let him move to another place" — he should choose to exile himself to a place of Torah. As he will then make sure that his sons will be Torah scholars; and he will also learn the laws and the statutes and go in the path of the good. And Rabbi Yose ben Kisma spoke well (Avot 6:9): "Even if you were to give me all the silver and gold, precious stones and pearls that are in the world, I would not dwell anywhere except in a place of Torah." As if he will learn one good thing [there], it is enough for him. And included in this is one who wants to merit the crown of Torah but does not find from whom to learn in his place. His father should send him, or he should go himself, to a city of sages and scribes to study Torah. And he should not be concerned about the strain or the separation, or about the expense. That is since everything [else] is like nothing compared to the good of meriting the crown of Torah. And even if there is a sage in his city, he can sometimes learn better in another city. And it is as the Tosafot wrote (Tosafot on Shabbat 9b:7, s.v. Ha lan) that the custom of the early scholars was like this, that those from the land of Israel would go to Babylonia to be focused without a disturbance.

And included in the commandment of loving the convert (literally, stranger) is to help  and assist a person who is wandering from his place and lives in a foreign land. And it is not specifically [dealing with] a convert. For is 'the resident on the ground and the stranger in the highest heavens' [such that there is no reason to assist the stranger]? And go after the reason - as it is written (Exodus 23:9), "for you know the feelings of the stranger, having yourselves been strangers in the land of Egypt." Behold it is explicit that the verse is referring to someone who lives in a foreign land without a companion or brother, and who has no acquaintances, such that his spirit is lowly and his heart is broken and depressed. It is fitting to have mercy upon [such a person] and to bring him close and to be his friend and companion, and to help him and support him regarding everything that comes his way. And with this, one fulfills this great commandment.

Civility [Derekh Eretz]: The branches and details of civility are many, the teaching of civility being broader than the heavens and the earth. Is it not written about in the words of our Rabbis, may their memory be blessed, in Tractate Derekh Eretz; and further explained in the books of the masters of ethics [mussar], such as the holy book, Reishit Chochmah at the end, the book Shnei Luchot HaBrit, and the book, Shevet Mussar (Chapter 16) in the [ethical] will attributed to R. Eliezer the Great? Whoever is someone who desires life (alluding to Psalms 34:13) should study the refined search to guard the path to the tree of life (alluding to Genesis 3:24). For they truly said (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3), "Civility preceded the Torah." And especially someone who is in the category of a Torah scholar — if he does not have civility, behold, he desecrates God and the Torah. And we have learned (Avot 3:10), "Anyone from whom the spirit of creations find pleasure, from him the spirit of God finds pleasure." And this is the great principle about civility: One should do what is good and straight in the eyes of God and man, negate his will before the will of others, and have an awareness of other people. And one has not fulfilled his obligation with all that a person learns about the laws of civility until he becomes wise and understands [what to do] on his own. For these are things that have no measure. Rather, everything is according to the place and the time, and according to who he is as a person, to interact with each person according to their traits and to get to what the other is really thinking and to do his will if it is not against the will of the Creator.

Evil speech is the head root sprouting poison (alluding to Deuteronomy 29:17), for its severity corresponds to that of idolatry, sexual immorality, and murder [put together] (Arkahin 15b). And King David, peace be upon him, has already expunged it, as it is written: May the Lord expunge all flattering lips, every tongue that speaks arrogance (Psalms 12:4). And evil speech is when one speaks disparagingly about his fellow. If it is something that has nothing to it, it is also called putting out a bad name. But if it is true, it is called evil speech – anything that was not known and this one reveals it. A talebearer reveals secrets (alluding to Proverbs 11:13), as he carries things to and fro and says, “X did this to you,” or “said this and that about you.” Their tongue is a sharpened arrow (alluding to Jeremiah 9:7); their throat is an open grave (alluding to Psalms 5:10). However, if he sees that damage will come to his fellow, he is obligated to reveal it to him so that he can be on guard. About this is it stated: You are not to traffic in slander among your kinspeople, you are not to stand by the blood of your neighbor; I am the Lord (Leviticus 19:16).

And it is [good to add ethical teachings] especially when reading the Haggadah on the night of Passover, which is a commandment from the Torah - as it is written (Exodus 13:8), "And you shall tell your son." 'And anyone who adds [and spends extra time] in telling the story of the exodus from Egypt, behold he is praiseworthy.' And the main part of the commandment is to tell over in fine detail, to his children and his wife, the deeds of the Lord and to add in the telling over of the Omnipresent's praise and the magnitude of His ability and providence over the individual; and of His great love, affection and compassion - 'and how many goodly aspects did the Omnipresent bestow upon us!' And hence an obligation rests upon us to fear and love God, and to serve Him with complete service. These are all outgrowths (lit., fruits) of the Haggadah.

The letter "Yud": REVERENCE - with reverence you cannot go wrong because it to guards against all evil. It is known that there is an external reverence, which fears punishment in this world and the next, for many pains afflict the wicked and reproofs for sin, to the extent that no one can fathom the great evil that the soul of the wicked endures in the world to come. They say that if a person were to suffer in his life as Job suffered, it would not be as a drop in the sea against the anguish of the day of death. And all the anguish of the day of death is not as a drop in the sea against the sufferings of the world to come, which empower the wicked to endure their suffering. Those who pass through the valley of weeping shall turn it into a spring (Psalm 84:7). Our sages, may their memory be a blessing, interpreted (Eruvin 19a) that we cause rivers of tears to flow. Indeed, a person must, while in this world, protection for his soul and consider the benefit for a transgression relative to its loss. He should have complete faith and believe that the Holy One, blessed be He, doesn’t become permissive even for  the smallest moment.

And so it was that a single soul was developed to the Holy Rabbi Reishit Chochma, Hashem diligently scrutinizes humanity from the realm above far more than one could fathom, and it is the divine decree to mete out justice upon all. Therefore, the man who possesses reverence and a tender heart shall be cautious and guard against every transgression as if evading a sword. And if by chance he stumbles and falls into sin, let him hasten to find refuge until the days of adversity and remorse shall no longer avail. As long as there remains strength within him, whatever he can accomplish, he shall indeed do. However, observe that this fear is referred to as "evil fear" in the Holy Zohar, for it is found that one does not fear the Lord Himself, but rather fears for his own soul. Nevertheless, even this type of fear is considered good, for through acting ‘not for the sake of Heaven’ turns into ‘acting for the sake of Heaven,’ one attains righteousnes. But truly pure is the fear of the Lord, which is the awe of His supernal majesty, for He is great, mighty, and beyond comprehension. His attributes and knowledge are immeasurable and incalculable. Yet not all individuals merit to attain such fear; rather, it depends on their awakening and deeds. It is contingent upon their diligent study of spiritual books on the Wisdom and on the reverence of the Lord.

The essence beheld in all matters of sanctity lies within one's utmost diligence and vigilance. It is known that the commandment to fear the revered and awe-inspiring Lord is one of the 613 commandments, and abundant it is. This is a constant commandment, for at any given moment when one remembers to fear the Lord, they fulfill a direct biblical commandment. A person cannot claim that they wished to fulfill a commandment but were unable to do so, for there are commandments that are dependent on thought and remembrance, which are within one's capacity to fulfill every moment. Whether at home on the Sabbath, while traveling on the road, amidst the company of others, or engrossed in one's business affairs while seated in a shop or the like, one should not incline their heart towards idleness, but rather cultivate pure thoughts, thereby fulfilling a commandment. The Holy One, blessed be He, rewards such endeavors.

What a pleasure it is to utter, again and again, the timeless verse "I have set the Lord always before me" (Psalms 16:8). It is truly exceptional how the Divine Name can be inscribed within one's consciousness, in a manner that fosters a sense of reverence. Indeed, the holy Ari, may his memory be a blessing, taught that it is possible to cultivate such awe-inspiring awareness. (I have witnessed individuals who would write these three sacred words – YHVH, ahava (love), and yir'ah (fear) – on a piece of parchment or paper, binding it beneath their fingers in a way that it remains concealed, serving as a constant reminder in their midst during Shabbat in their homes and journeys as well.) This commandment of reverence leads to further benefits, as it safeguards one from all evil. Fortunate is the person who harbors perpetual fear, for it is within this state that they prevent any anguish or wrath from affecting the exalted and awesome King. They tremble and repent from wrongdoing, choosing to do good and bring solace to their Creator.

Money/silver - it is written "The tongue of the just is like choice silver" (Prov. 10:20) and it is also written "under the shadow of wisdom, under the shadow of silver" (Eccl. 7:12). Look and see the analogy of silver to speech and of silver to wisdom. There is a hint there, that they said "life and death are in the hands of the tongue, one who wants who live can do so because of the tongue, one who wants to die can do so because of the tongue" (Arakhin 15b). And they also said that the Torah is similar to a simple drug one who wants life [can get it through Torah] one who wants death [can get it through Torah] (Kidushin 30b). So too this we can say about the question of money: one who wants who live can do so because of the money, one who wants to die can do so because of the money - this is because most of the transgressions are caused due to a person being eager after money: robbing, stealing, exploitation, cheating, swearing falsely, swearing a lie, lies, unrighteousness in character traits [NT: could be 'in judgment' as עול במשפט makes more sense in the context of Torah list], moving boundaries, disputes, jealousy, hatred, rivalry, forbidden foods, desecration of Shabbat and holy days, and most of the transgressions that a person does is over gaining money, and the sin of desecrating God's Name is on top of them all. And so too, someone who loves their money cancels most of the mitzvot and the prayers and the blessings, and study of Torah corresponds to them all. And when such a person does them, they are unfit due to the doing them as fast as possible, and with miserliness, and the fact that one's heart is not into it, since that person's heart is only preoccupied with their own gain all the time, and they avert their eyes from [the needy by not giving] tzedakah, and when this person wants to do it, they really don't, and likewise many evils are done this way "riches kept for their owner to the owner's pwn hurt" (Eccl. 5:12) and at its hands one inherits Gehenna and goes down to the pit of destruction.

And in truth they said "a person is known through his pocket" (Eruvin 65b). Truly, the desire for money is a formidable adversary, especially in this generation, which is a generation focused on money, in which a person can be more eager for money than for any other transgression and any other pleasure, and the money of a person can be more dear to some than their bodies and even their souls. But this is the Torah for people in this world, that one should conquer their desires (Avot 4:1) and open their eyes and see that silver collects souls, gold grieves souls, and they will understand that this is truthful truth, because it is better for a person to die of hunger and not be evil in the presence of the Place and not anger their Creator, God forbid.

And were it possible to conquer one's impulse by force and that money should be seen in one's eyes as nothing in comparison to doing the Creator's will! Therefore, one should look at money as stones to do our Heavenly Parent's will. And should should believe with perfect faith, and set it in one's heart with immovable nails that the amount of one's food is defined by Heaven. Even if they went to heaven or went down to the deepest depths, no one could add or subtract even a cent [to this quantity] with the exception of the outlays of mitzvot and good deeds which are not defined, rather on this case if a person adds, they add to that person. And therefore one who acquires their world through their money by doing lots of tzedakah, mitzvot and good deeds, and  acquires a good name for themselves, and acquires words of Torah, and acquires for oneself life of the world to come. And the mnemonic: 'word of Torah, coins acquired' (Eruvin 81b, Bava Kamma 46b, Bava Kamma 47b and other places) that for all words of Torah and for all good things one needs coins, and money will answer all. One who is wise will guard these words and won't go to sleep. End of all words, all was heard, fear God and guard God's mitzvot, since this is all that there is to being human (Eccl. 12:13)

Love for a perfect king who abundantly does good, who chooses His people Israel with love. Through His love and compassion, He bestows upon us countless blessings that cannot be comprehended. And above all, He chose us from among all the nations and sanctified us with His commandments. It is stated in the Zohar that any commandment that is not performed with awe and love is not a true commandment and does not ascend on high. Specifically, in the study of Torah and its hidden aspects, if one does not hear its voice with awe and love, as it is written (Numbers 11:1), 'And the Lord heard, and His anger was kindled,' Heaven forbid.

It is appropriate to study all the books of ethics, one after the other and constantly review them. This is 'a statute not to be transgressed,' day after day, night after night. And even when one reviews books that he already read, they will be like new in his eyes and bring new inspiration according to the time and the state of his soul. For not all times are the same, as 'the righteous one will distinguish.' And since they said 'things that came out from the heart, which will penetrate the heart,' how fine is it to study Pirkei Avot, all the ethics in the Talmud and Midrash, the holy book, Reishit Chochmah, the book of the pious rabbi, Shnei Luchot HaBrit and the many similar holy books, they are all holy! (And if God will be with me, I will collect the words of ethics in short form from all of the holy books, words that pierce the heart, a word in its time, and translate them. May God make it complete for me and help me for the matter of the glory of His name.) And those who read in foreign languages should seek and pursue books in foreign languages, such as Tikkun HaNefesh, Shevet Mussar, and that which is similar to them, like 'one who pursues a partridge in the hills,' and seek to listen to their teachings.

Pain - It is not proper to regret anything in the world except for “sorrow of heaven” [i.e. causing sorrow to Hashem, in an anthropomorphic sense, by not following his will], for due to the emptiness of the world there is no room for distress, for all is vanity [Ecclesiastes 1:2]. And we already have a parable about why the Holy One, blessed be He, does not pity the suffering of the righteous, whether others cause them pain or they are troubled over the circumstances of the time. This is similar to a father who watches his son as a baby, build a house out of small sticks and straw and be happy with it. Then a man comes and destroys the house. The child goes to his father and complains to him about the man and cries bitterly, and thinks that the father should kill that man, but the father laughs and does not pay attention, for he knows that in truth the pain of his child is vain and empty. Rather, this great distress is all due to [the child’s] limited knowledge and comprehension. For the pain that distresses man in his eyes in this world, is all vanity and striving after wind. And as at times the father supports his son to build these little houses, and buys things that bring joy to his children and gives him pleasure according to his [the child’s] own understanding, so too the Holy One, blessed be He, at times fulfills the will of man regarding matters of this world according to his [the person’s] understanding, because his soul desires them, in order to give him satisfaction. And if the Holy One, blessed be He, pains someone through afflictions to atone for his sins and he suffers and cries, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not heed his distress even though the Master of Mercy is merciful and gracious. After all, this is similar to a child whose mother is bathing him from his filth and he screams and cries; his mother is not distressed over this. And just as a physician makes difficult remedies, and at times cuts of a limb, and isn’t distressed over the pain, for he knows that this is for [the patient’s] pleasure and benefit, so too everything the Merciful One does, He does for the good. And a man who understands this ought not to be distressed at all.

And the book “Shnei Luchot Haberit [The Two Tablets of the Covenant]” recounts an incident regarding one pious person that entered a city and saw them troubled and embittered, and he became happy and cheerful and danced gleefully. And the people of the city asked him, “why are you happy?” He said to them, “why not be happy?” They said to him, “don’t you see everyone weeping in front of their tents? Why are you laughing while everyone is crying?” He said to them that this is like a parable: [if] one entered the house and found them [the inhabitants] sleeping and dreaming frightening dreams, and crying in their dreams, would the one who see this be distressed? For he knows this is nothing but a dream, and when the sleeper awakens he will be at ease. So too here, as all that causes distress in this world is like a dream, and I, being awake, know that all is vanity. Rather over the sorrow of heaven one is obligated to be distressed, and from this follows every kind of sorry that one out to feel over sins, iniquities, and transgressions. Not [grieving] over the harsh punishments that he himself receives, but rather that he caused sorrow and angered the King of Glory.

And thus it is proper to be distressed over the destruction of the Beit Hamikdash [temple] which was destroyed due to our sins, not because we are exiled, pained, and downtrodden, but rather due to the sorrow of heaven which is very great. And similarly over all types of afflictions, this should be one’s sorrow: that he causes anger and pain to the High and Exalted King, as is written (Isaiah 63:9): “in all their affliction he is afflicted”. And this is similar to a son who loves his father and angers him greatly until the father is forced to forsake his kindness and strike him with a great blow, for if the son is a loyal lover he wouldn’t worry about his blows at all, rather [he would worry] over the anger and distress of his father, and think, what will I do and how will I reconcile with my father so that he will not have sorrow and anger because of me. And even more so [we should be distressed due to] our knowledge that the mercy of Heaven is great, and that He bestows good without end, and great is His love for his people Israel. And his sorrow over their suffering is [also] vast, as is written (Exodus 19:21) “and many of them perish”. And our rabbis of blessed memory explain [the verse] (Mechilta on Parsha Yitro 84), that if even one falls, it is in his eyes as if many [have fallen]. If so, it is proper to be distressed over afflictions, on the one hand, since certainly our Father in Heaven is greatly angered, to the point that he was compelled to strike him with a great blow. And at the time when a person suffers, the Divine Presence suffers — what does the phrase say? “My head is heavy” etc. [Sanhedrin 46a]

And this is why one must feel genuine pain in their soul over the passing of the righteous, and over all the afflictions of the righteous that are wounded for our transgressions and broken for our sins. And because of [impending] evil the righteous are gathered, and the pain of heaven increases since the people of faith are gone, who come [to pray] in the power of their [good] deeds, etc. etc. And one must be distressed even over the righteous who died in antiquity, as is said (Zohar Part 3 Page 57), all that mourn over the deaths of the sons of Aaron on Yom Kippur, all their sins are forgiven. And this is the meaning of “the living shall take it to heart” [Ecclesiastes 7:2] — “if a flame has fallen among the cedars, what shall the wall-hyssop do?” [Moed Katan 25b]. And further one should take to heart that due to our great sins the faithful disappear from the children of man, and the pious are lost from the earth and men have no strength. And the Holy One, blessed be He, has no people in this world to love as in the days of old and in the years of antiquity. And this is because of our sins as is said in Gemara (Sanhedrin 11a): So-and-so Rabbi was worthy that the Divine Presence rest upon him, except that his generation was not worthy of it. And because of the decline of the generations, the Torah continues to diminish, progressively decreasing. Over this, it is fitting to feel bitterness and to grieve with a writing sorrow.

And as is written in Kabbalah, the sins of the wicked and the strengthening of the kelipot due to them [the wicked] causes confusion in the thoughts of the righteous, as they are unable to serve their creator completely and cleave to him as is proper. Therefore, our hearts should tremble over this to their very core, and we should weep bitterly over this great evil, and over the great evil and suffering that is caused above [in Heaven] due to our sins.

And behold, if a man is distressed over the vanities of this world, this [reflects] a deficiency of understanding, as we have written above in the name of the author of “Sefer HaBerit”. For either way, if it is something that has a remedy, he should do the remedy and he will be rescued, and if there is no remedy, what will [his distress] give him, what will it add, and what benefit is there in his sorrow? But he should be distressed over the sorrow of Heaven, [for] his distress makes an impression and bears fruit. It makes an impression, for this is the way of the world [i.e. proper conduct] and part of the perfection of one’s character traits, that a person’s disposition should be engaged with others. And he should be distressed, or at the very least display distress, and weep with those who weep. And how much disgrace comes to those who go to a funeral, and while the grave is prepared, the relatives of the deceased sit by the deceased with embittered spirits, and they [the funeral goers] engage excessively in drinking, laughter, and frivolity, at that very time and place in the presence of the deceased and his relatives. Certainly the matter is very disgraceful, bad, and bitter. And it is proper to protest against them if they will listen. Let this bad custom disappear, and let there not be such a thing among Israel.

And moreover, if one’s father, mother, or relatives are suffering, one is obligated to be distressed over them. And this is half of the consolation of a person: that he sees that others are also distressed over his pain. Along these lines, a person who is distressed over the sorrow of heaven, proportional to his suffering he brings satisfaction to his creator, and proportional to the pain is the reward. And it bears fruit, for proportional to his suffering he increasingly tries to straighten that which he has perverted and does everything in his power to lessen the suffering of his father in Heaven, just as a son who loves his father and sees him in pain, writhing in his suffering, whose flesh aches upon him [Job 14:22], and who endangers his life to save him from his suffering. And as the Kabbalists have already written, proportional to the pain and groaning and suffering that one experiences over his sins, thus so he increasingly purifies his soul. Behold, how precious indeed are the words of the wise man (Mivchar HaPeninim 44:46), who said to someone who he saw in distress, if your pain is about things in this world, the Holy One, blessed be He, will remove your distress, and if it is over the sorrow of Heaven, the Holy One, blessed be He, will add more and more sorrow to you.

And behold, the matter of distress is something entrusted to the heart. And the “nearby inclination” [i.e. the Yetzer Hara] reverses things and brings sorrow over the vanities of this world, while the sorrow of Heaven is discarded from the heart; [he is] neither pained nor aware. And the pure man should strengthen himself with pure thoughts to do each thing at its proper time in its proper manner, not replacing or substituting it, and he who comes to purify receives [heavenly] assistance (Shabbat 104a). And know that which is written in Ben Sira (Yevamot 63b) “do not suffer from tomorrow’s trouble etc.”. And since our days are a shadow on the earth [I Chronicles 29:15], what is the benefit to man in all his toils if his life will be [one of] sorrow? There is no good for man unless he is happy with his portion, trusts in the Name [i.e. Hashem], and does good [deeds].

However, there is [also] good jealousy, like the statement of our rabbis, may their memory be blessed (Bava Batra 21a), "The jealousy of scribes [towards each other] increases wisdom." [As one] will desire and put their efforts into moving up in levels of wisdom and of serving God, may His name be blessed, like the holy ones that are in the land (alluding to Psalms 16:3). So a person is obligated to say, "When will my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 25). And when he sees that his fellow is successful in his actions, this should be his jealousy — that he says, "Everything is certainly according to the deeds of a person, he shall eat the fruits of his deeds." So his heart should be jealous with the fear of God, in the way that it is written (Genesis 30:1): and Rachel was jealous of her sister. And our rabbis, may their memory be blessed, explained (Bereishit Rabbah 71:6) that she was jealous of her good deeds. As she said, "If she were not better than I, she would not have merited to be built up [by bearing children]." And through this, one will improve his deeds to please the spirit of his Maker, since that is all of man (alluding to Ecclesiastes 12:13).

Constancy: The designation of set times for Torah [study] is one of the things that they ask a man on the day of judgment — did you set fixed times for Torah (Shabbat 31b). Accordingly, the book Chok LeYisrael has now become well-known in all of the diaspora of Israel. And it is one of the things wherein the little holds much, and is very important. For in a little time, one engages in many types of study, and his hand is in everything (alluding to Genesis 16:12). And it was set up according to the esoteric understanding by the cubs of the Ari, may his memory be blessed. He builds his rafters in the Heavens (alluding to Psalms 104:2-3) and learns wisdom, ethics, and laws from it. And how good and how pleasant (alluding to Psalms 133:1) is the custom of some cities, such that they gather as a group of those that fear God and esteem His name, to study the order of Chok LeYisrael. And the sage among them reads out loud and explains the law to them, and sometimes the holy Zohar, and the [book] Yosef LeChok. In this way, everyone — even the most ignorant — can merit to learn this study after the verses. Additionally, there is the virtue of this study being in a group and the saying of Kaddish. And this study is so very important.

Healing - Our sages of blessed memory said on the verse "And heal he will be healed" [shemot 21;19] - from here the Torah gave the permission to doctors to heal. [berakhot 60a] And it is also said [with respect to illnesses] - that they are bad and trustworthy [Deut / devarim 28;59] - that they are "trustworthy" as an emissary / delegate [of heaven] [rashi there] for at the time that they are appointed / delegated [to fall upon a person] - it is decreed upon them that they should only leave on a determined day by the appointed doctor using the prescribed medicine. Our sages have also said "A person should not live in a place where there is no doctor" [sanhedrin 17b]

And thus we find that an [interesting] inquiry arises. Since it is Hashem who determines death and life - what what will the doctor add [by aiding to heal the patient]? Is it not so that if it was decreed [in Heaven] that one will die, even if all the doctors in the world arose to heal him, they would not be able to save him from death?And thus [we can better understand] our sages statement "the error / malpractice of the doctor is the will of the Creator" and it is not in his power to save. And if it was decreed upon the person that he should live, even without a doctor, the Holy One Blessed Be He, will turn over [worlds] and cure him. For Hashem has many ways and with Him there is much deliverance and He will stretch out his word [other version "hand"] and heal him. However, the answer to this inquiry and to many others like it is that there are three different types of decrees - 1) If he is one that holds a special merit and his merit is strong and his fate is salutary - even if he doesn't have a doctor and he does things that will worsen his condition, he will not die and "live he will live". 2) And there are those, upon whom death is decreed - that is to say, even if he guarded himself with all protection in the world, his persistence of protecting himself is all in vain, and doctors will be of no help and he will not be saved. 3) However, there are those who, due to their sins, place themselves under the influence of "nature": - if they protect themselves and act with the proper cures according to nature - "live he will live" - he will surely live.  - and if not they will die and on this type of person it is said "and there is death without judgment."

Behold, thus each person needs to seek the proper cure when he needs them. For if he will not do this and will cause "death without judgment", he will be held accountable for his life. And he is at fault [his death is worthwhile] for he transgressed on that that is written [in the Torah], "and you shall protect very well your life." [deut / devarim 4;15]  And the person who does not preserve his health, and does not act in the according to nature, to seek the proper medical treatment of his illness, to the best of his ability - will surely be punished since he transgressed that which is written in the Torah. It also comes out that he depended on a miracle and if a miracle was done for him, a part of his merits will be taken away.

One needs to be very careful to guard one's health so that he will not become ill. And if he did become sick, he needs to seek cures and consult expert physicians. And he should not be concerned about his money [he will spend for the cure], for a person should give all his money to save his life. As it says in the Zohar HaKadosh "that one who is apt to suffer monetary loss, he will fall into house of illness, and will not be cured until the amount that it was decreed for him to lose, is spent." That is why it is good advice to spend the money as quickly as possible. And how good is it for a person to increase his giving of charity - for he gains a mitzvah and it is a segulah (an ability) to nullify the decree [of suffering]. Really, before a person should seek cures - he should always believe with complete conviction - that his healing is in the hands of the Holy One Blessed be He - the Merciful and Trustworthy Physician - Healer of Israel, His people. Thus, he should preface [his acts], with prayer before Him. (And I already composed a prayer for an ill person and placed it in my place of prayer)

A person who has a sick person in his household, is obligated not to slumber, and not to remain silent, and not to rest until he seeks all types of doctors and all sorts of remedies according to his means / until he achieves his objective. And if he is a needy person, and he cannot afford [proper diagnosis and treatment], the obligation falls on the citizens of his city and/or on the Bikur Holim Organization (lit - visitation of the ill society - ie, the illness relief fund). - to assign for him doctors and cures - and they should not be concerned about the great expenses, for they should consider how great is the mitzvah. Go and learn till where the obligation to heal applies, for behold they permitted our holy / strict Shabbat to be desecrated and to transgress upon the entire Torah in order to treat a person who was in mortal danger. As our the Talmud says "It is better for one to desecrate one Shabbat so that one may observe many other Shabbats." [shabbat 151a] And how much more so that it is proper to spend all the money in the world in order to save one Jewish soul - for it is as if one saved the entire world. And even if with all this effort the person still passed away, G-d forbid, this should not serve to make them regret and balk (at the money spent). Rather they should rejoice in their hearts knowing they did did what was required of them to do. To Hashem - they are doing the best that they can do - and Hashem will pay them seven times over in their laps with wealth and riches in their home.

Pele Yoetz – on Sinah - Hatred - Hatred [of others] is hated [by Hash-m] for upon it the Tanna said Rabbi Yehoshua says a bad eye & the evil inclination & hatred of the creatures [of Hash-m], expel a person from the world. (Pirkei Avot 2:11 on Self-Destruction And it causes many sins for hatred awakens quarrels & one falls into the grips of controversy & evil speech & causes one to become happy for the misfortune [of others] & to damage & cause pain & to take vengeance & to spite like a snake [against the other] & many similar evils. And it is written in the holy books – that there is no sin of all the sins like hatred – because every moment one transgresses upon that that is written in the Torah “Do not hate your brother in your heart.” and that that is written “You shall love your fellow as yourself.” & this is the reason why gratuitous hatred destroyed the Holy Temple. And any kind of of hatred is considered 'gratuitous hatred', for any kind of claims that he has [against the other party] to express, are vanity, acts of delusion, like we explained above in the section of 'love of [our] fellows' - see there.

"Especially how much more so should a person rejoice over the many rational mitzvot and human pleasures, such as the one who opens a shop and blesses his Creator for his enjoyments and kindnesses. And the one who prays and asks for his needs and the like, it is considered a mitzvah and brings satisfaction to his Creator and sets a reward for him. Is there a taste more delightful than this? Similarly, eating and drinking on Shabbat and Yom Tov and the mitzvah of marital relations and the like, it is considered a mitzvah and brings satisfaction to his Creator and sets a reward for him. Is there a taste sweeter than this? Even in worldly matters, such as eating, drinking, sleeping, and conducting business, if done for the sake of Heaven, it is considered a mitzvah and one receives a reward. For this, Israel should rejoice greatly in their Maker, it is impossible not to rejoice. However, one must pay attention and strengthen oneself in pure thoughts in the manner that we say, 'Blessed is the person who listens to Your commandments and sets Your Torah and Your word upon his heart.'And regarding what is before us, look and see that as much as a person rejoices over the great goodness that God has done for Israel and sanctified us with His commandments, it is considered a mitzvah and brings satisfaction to his Creator and sets a reward for him. Is there a taste sweeter than this? Fortunate are we, how good is our portion and how pleasant is our lot. Our sages of blessed memory said (Kiddushin 39b) that the reward for a mitzvah does not exist in this world. But for the joy, a person eats in this world. And the greatest reward for joy is that one merits to attain wisdom and achieve perfection, as revealed by our teacher, the holy Ari, of blessed memory, that what he attained of wonderful wisdom and the Holy Spirit was all because he rejoiced greatly in his engagement in Torah and fulfilling any mitzvah more than finding great spoils. Thus, the reward for the joy of a mitzvah is itself a mitzvah."

Six - Regarding the number six the Kabbalists wrote that one needs to be very careful to say, "hashishi" [the sixth], for it is the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and his Shekhinah [Divine Presence]. And thus one should also be careful in writing. For example when writing a Ketubah on the sixth day, he should write "bayom hashishi" [on the sixth day], and when writing chapters he should write "perek hashishi" [the sixth chapter]. And in everything similar to this, one should always be careful in this. And especially when he recites the song of the levites, he should say "hayom yom hashishi" [today is the sixth day], and he should have the intention to unite the Holy One, blessed be He, and his Shekhinah, Yesod and Malchut [foundation and kingship], and these matters are ancient.
